News.title: Trump lawyers in uproar as judge rules they must hand his financial records to BBC in defamation case
News.content:
Trump lawyers in uproar as judge rules they must hand his financial records to BBC in defamation case

The judge said that, in order to show the 'reputational and financial injury' to Trump from the 2024 Panorama documentary, his legal team must hand over financial records to the BBC's lawyers

View Image The president's lawyers are not happy at the decision (file photo) (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

A judge has ruled that Donald Trump must hand over his financial records to the BBC as part of his 10 billion dollar (£7.5 billion) defamation case against the broadcaster.

‌



Trump’s legal team has tried to block the move, calling the ruling “premature, improper, and especially burdensome”.

‌



It comes after Trump sued the UK broadcaster in a Florida court over the editing of a Panorama documentary from 2024 about the US Capitol riots.

‌



BBC lawyers had asked for the financial documents from the Donald J Trump Revocable Trust, which holds the president’s business interests and assets. Judge Enjolique Lett granted the request for access to records from the trust, which is managed by Trump’s eldest son.

Trump’s representatives had called the BBC team’s request a “fishing expedition”, a claim rejected by BBC lawyers, who said the details were needed to assess the financial impact of the programme.

‌



The court papers stated: “Defendants have requested information from these entities only because plaintiff alleges without limitation that his financial interests have been impacted by defendants’ actions and because plaintiff is the sole beneficiary of a trust that owns or is associated with nearly 400 entities.”

The trust, which is also represented by Mr Trump’s lawyers, had sought to resist the demand previously arguing: “Although plaintiff has alleged that his businesses have suffered damages as a result of the documentary, that alone does not give defendants carte-blanche to obtain sweeping financial discovery from hundreds of non-parties.”

Trump’s lawsuit alleged that the Panorama episode, broadcast shortly before the 2024 presidential election he won, caused him reputational and financial injury. Criticism has been levelled at the show claiming it gave the impression the US president had encouraged his supporters to storm the Capitol building on January 6 2021 after he lost the election to Joe Biden.

Article continues below

BBC director-general Tim Davie resigned in the wake of the allegations and BBC chairman Samir Shah apologised on behalf of the broadcaster over an “error of judgment”. Mr Shah accepted the editing of the programme gave “the impression of a direct call for violent action”.

But the corporation is fighting to have the case thrown out of court, claiming that it will have a “chilling effect” it would have on “robust reporting on public figures and events”.

It has also challenged the jurisdiction of a Florida court to hear the case given the programme was never aired in the state or the US.

News.title: Donald Trump threatens to blow up 'bridge or power plant' every time Iran hits ship
News.content:
Donald Trump threatens to blow up 'bridge or power plant' every time Iran hits ship

US President Donald Trump has thrashed out plans for Iran ground invasion as he warned Tehran he will blow up a bridge or a power depot every time they hit a ship in the Strait of Hormuz

View 3 Images Donald Trump speaks during a reception with FIFA President Gianni Infantino last week (Image: AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)

US President Donald Trump has threatened to blow up a power plant or bridge every time Iran hits a ship in the latest Middle East crisis escalation.

‌



It came as it emerged Pentagon war-planners are drafting a scheme for a partial ground invasion of Iran if the Tehran regime refuses to back down. The President has not green-lighted a ground assault on key Kharg Island but it is one of the options for escalation with which he has been presented.

‌



Mr Trump stormed: "From this point forward, any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by missile, rocket, drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy one bridge or power plant, including those located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran."

‌



In recent weeks, the Republican leader has made repeated threats against civilian infrastructure as he became frustrated with Iran’s defiance.

Zelensky fires Ukraine's military chief after widespread protests READ MORE :

View 3 Images A plane being prepared for war (Image: X)

But Iran has hit back with warnings of their own escalation, claiming they could attack US bases and even kidnap US soldiers, whisking them back to Tehran. And Tehran’s military even threatened that it America does occupy Khark Island then Iran would go ahead and bomb its own territory. Former Iranian Foreign Minister Manouchehr Mottaki, now a member of parliament, said Iran should go further than striking US bases in the region and consider capturing American soldiers.

‌



He stormed: "The US threats have intensified, and it has said that it will seize Kharg Island and take control of Iran's oil facilities. I have been advocating for a ground war for a long time. We should seize one of the US bases in the region, capture its forces, and bring them back to our country.’ An Iranian army spokesperson warned Iran would bomb its own territory rather than allow US forces to occupy it, as threats of a ground operation grown.

Brigadier General Mohammad Akrami-Nia said on Iranian state television: “If America occupies our territory, we will even bomb our own territory. This is the logic of war." The remarks came as US Central Command marked the tenth consecutive day of strikes against Iranian targets. US President Donald Trump is expected to decide in the coming days how to proceed, with the prospect of a US ground operation or seizure of Iranian territory now openly discussed.The Pentagon is preparing options for ground operations in Iran that would fall short of a full invasion but could involve thousands of troops and take weeks or months.

View 3 Images Bridge hit by US in Iran strikes (Image: ISNA/AFP via Getty Images)

Article continues below

The White House said the Pentagon was working to give the president "maximum optionality" but that "this does not mean the president has made a decision." Iranian MP Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a former member of the parliamentary National Security Commission, said Tehran could launch ground attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain if the US invaded Iranian territory. On the prospect of a US assault on Kharg Island, he said Washington might take it for a day but could not hold it. He said: "Iranian missiles from Semnan, Zahedan, Isfahan and elsewhere can reach it. Occupying Kharg Island would turn it into a target for Iran.”

And it is possible Iran could make a bold move to take territory, including the taking of Bubiyan Island which is owned by Kuwait. The island, with an area of 700 square mikles, is Kuwait's largest and sits at the northern end of the Persian Gulf close to Iraq. Some Iranian political figures and social media accounts have considered the scenario in response to a potential US seizure of Kharg, suggesting the IRGC could use regional proxies and its Saberin special forces unit to launch a ground operation through southern Iraq if Washington moved on Iranian territory.

The Saberin unit is an elite IRGC formation with extensive combat experience across Iran and neighbouring countries. Reports of Iranian military movements toward the Kuwaiti border have circulated online. Kuwait hosts US forces and has been among the most heavily targeted countries in the latest wave of Iranian strikes. Earlier reports in March and May alleged that IRGC commandos had targeted Bubiyan and engaged against Kuwaiti forces.

News.title: PC Harper's widow criticises early prisoner release plan as Burnham to review scheme
News.content:
The widow of PC Andrew Harper has described the possible early release of prisoners as "deplorable", following reports that two of his killers could be freed early.

Lissie Harper said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham earlier said he would review the Sentencing Act policy that from September would see thousands of offenders in England and Wales eligible to be released earlier.

Speaking on Wednesday, Burnham said: "I can't say that I can change the policy completely, but I will look at it in detail before we go further forward."

He acknowledged that there was "pressure on prisons places" and that a failure to invest in the prison system in the past had created "an unacceptable situation".

Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter but could be released early under the new Sentencing Act.

PC Harper was killed after he was dragged to his death behind their getaway car. The car's driver, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for manslaughter but would not be eligible for early release.

Burnham's comments came after the mother of police officer Andrew Harper said the potential early release of two of her son's killers felt like an "insult".

In a separate statement released later on Wednesday, PC Harper's widow Lissie Harper said: "It has taken me years to rebuild a life that was torn apart in a matter of moments. Years to pick up the pieces left behind by three men whose actions robbed Andrew of his life and stole our future.

"It is deplorable to me that we have reached a point where releasing prisoners early is even considered acceptable. We speak of justice, accountability and standing with victims, yet decisions like this do the opposite."

The overcrowding of the prison estate has been a problem for several years and successive governments have released prisoners early in a bid to free up space.

Tens of thousands of inmates have been let out of prison to create more space in jails since 2024.

The Sentencing Act, which was passed by Sir Keir Starmer's government earlier this year, was designed to ease pressure on prisons, and will see some offenders spend less time in prison before release.

Burnham said: "I want to assure myself that everything has been looked at before this policy proceeds, and I can give that assurance that every single part of this I will look into with the justice secretary."

Concerning the case of PC Harper, he said: "I feel for the family it's an appalling crime that was committed."

He said the "main perpetrator" of his death would not be eligible for early release.

Burnham also said it was not acceptable to joke about early releases and that it was right Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had apologised for comments he made that were caught on camera.

News.title: Most bus fares in England to be capped at £2 from January
News.content:
The bus fare cap in England will revert to Â£2 from January, new prime minister Andy Burnham has announced.

The government says the policy, which is expected to cost more than Â£500m, will "help with the cost of living and give people the breathing space they need".

At the start of last year, the England-wide bus fare cap rose to Â£3 under Sir Keir Starmer's Labour government, although in Liverpool and Manchester fares were held at Â£2.

Burnham said affordable transport links were an essential, adding: "Lower fares will help people get to where they need to."

The measure gives people "a little bit of hope" in a time when many are grappling with higher living costs - especially after fuel costs spiked as a result of the US-Iran war, transport secretary Heidi Alexander told the BBC's Today programme.

However, she admitted the measure was "not the whole solution".

The new cap will take effect from January next year for fares on participating buses outside of London. The cost of a non-discounted single bus journey in London is Â£1.75.

The Burnham government said going back to a Â£2 cap should particularly help passengers in rural and coastal areas, where single fares can be higher.

The Campaign for Better Transport said rural areas were still suffering from fewer bus routes and services, adding that such areas had been more affected by council cut backs in the last decade than urban zones.

Services in those areas - as measured by vehicle miles - decreased by 18% between 2019 and 2024, according to the County Councils Network, which represents 39 unitary and county councils across England.

"What we need to see is the replacing of those lost services which have particularly affected those in rural areas," Campaign for Better Transport's Michael Solomon Williams said.

News.title: Ex-Southern Water boss among four charged over alleged plan to manipulate water quality tests
News.content:
The ex-chief executive of Southern Water has been charged with three others over an alleged plan to manipulate water quality tests to avoid paying financial penalties of about Â£45m, it can now be reported.

Matthew Wright is accused of conspiring to defraud the Environment Agency (EA) and water regulator Ofwat between 2012 and 2017, along with Philip Barker, Clive Massey and Mark Gregory, who also worked at the firm.

Wright's solicitor says he "denies all wrongdoing and has co-operated fully" with the EA's investigation.

Southern Water said the charges related to "a historic set of failures" uncovered in an internal investigation. It said it was a "completely different" company to a decade ago.

The EA asked a judge to issue a summons against the four, charging them with the offence, last year, but Wright launched a legal challenge, dismissed by two senior judges on Wednesday.

Massey, Gregory and Barker did not appear at the hearing in London and were not represented.

According to court documents, the allegations include arranging for wastewater to be removed from facilities by tankers in order to create "no flow" results.

This had been "with a view to covering up pollution and deceiving those whose function is to protect the public from such harm", prosecutors allege.

In his legal challenge, Wright's lawyers argued at the High Court in June that the EA did not have the power to issue the summons and it should be thrown out.

But the judges dismissed his claim and ruled restrictions previously preventing reporting of the legal challenge should be lifted.

Separate court listings showed the case against 60-year-old Wright, of Haslemere, Surrey; Barker, 57, of West Chiltington, West Sussex; Massey, 64, of Brandhill, Shropshire; and Gregory, 63, of Southampton, were scheduled to be heard at Medway Magistrates' Court on 14 July.

The four are accused of conspiring between 2012 and 2017 to defraud those conducting the environmental and financial regulation duties of Southern Water, including the EA and Ofwat, by "the implementation of artificial no-flow events at wastewater treatment works".

News.title: OpenAI says its AI went rogue and launched 'unprecedented' cyber-attack
News.content:
OpenAI has revealed some of its most advanced AI models went rogue and hacked a start-up after it lost control of them during a security test.

The ChatGPT-maker said its agent - an AI system which can operate alone after human instruction â was being tested in a controlled environment but, after finding weaknesses, was able to escape the test limits.

They targeted Hugging Face, one of the world's largest hubs for sharing AI models, gaining access to some internal company systems.

OpenAI said the incident was "unprecedented", external, and it was conducting an investigation alongside Hugging Face, whose boss Clement Delangue said in a post on X it was "mind-blowing that all of this happened autonomously".

"The investigation is ongoing, and we'll share more learnings from what might be the first incident of its kind," Delangue added.

A government spokesperson said the UK's AI Security Institute was studying the behaviour from the AI system seen in the incident and was continuing to work with OpenAI and other labs to improve safeguards.

They said organisations should step up their cyber-defences by taking steps such as enrolling in the government-backed Cyber Essentials certification scheme.

News.title: Prince George enjoys coastal fun in new video as he becomes a teenager
News.content:
A new video of Prince George has been released by Kensington Palace to mark his 13th birthday.

The video, external, showing a smiling prince waving at the camera in his sunglasses, playing cricket on the beach and climbing rocks, was accompanied by the caption: "Thank you for all the birthday wishes for George today!"

The video was shot in Cornwall at Easter, and follows a new photograph of George which was also published on social media on Wednesday.

George, the elder son of the Prince and Princess of Wales, is second in line to the throne.

News.title: Natalie Fleet leaves 'triggering' safeguarding minister role
News.content:
Natalie Fleet says she has stepped down as safeguarding minister after finding the role "overwhelmingly triggering", telling the BBC that it was making her ill.

The Labour MP, who was groomed and raped as a teenager, added she told the team of new Prime Minister Andy Burnham that she "sadly couldn't stay" in the job.

Fleet described it as the "bravest thing I've ever done" and offered her support to her successor.

She was appointed to the role on 12 May this year following the resignation of Jess Phillips, who said opportunities for progress had been "stalled and delayed" under the leadership of then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer.

Announcing her departure on the social media platform X, external, Fleet said: "Honour of lifetime to be minister for safeguarding. Quickly found contents overwhelmingly triggering."

She added: "Victims deserve someone at their best."

She told BBC News the nature of the role as safeguarding minister means "you hear the worst of humanity", saying: "I understand what it is like not to be seen and not to be heard."

"I know how important this job is and I know how much it needs a good and competent minister. It quickly became apparent how ill it was making me."

She received support from the Home Office while in post, she said.

"But even with that [support] the nature of the job means that you hear the worst of humanity.

"Anybody would struggle hearing that but not everyone would react in the same way as someone who has gone through what I have.

"For me it is one of the most important jobs in government. It was the honour of my life to be able to do it.

"Nothing can compare to being asked to make a difference to the lives of women and girls. It was incredible."

Fleet was elected MP for Bolsover in July 2024, succeeding Labour stalwart Dennis Skinner.

She has spoken openly about her experiences as a teenager, including in an interview with GB News in 2024.

Fleet said she became pregnant at the age of 15 after being groomed and raped by an older man, adding she has "weekly nightmares" about what she said happened to her.

"I didn't know we were having unprotected sex," she told the broadcaster. "I was a child and (it) is statutory rape."

The MP said she fell pregnant and gave birth to her daughter, who she described as the "absolute love of my life".

In her maiden speech in the House of Commons in October 2024, Fleet said it was her "duty" to speak up for women in her Derbyshire constituency "whose stories are not being told".

News.title: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to face trial next June
News.content:
The trial of ousted Venezuelan president NicolÃ¡s Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, is scheduled to begin on 1 June 2027, a New York judge ordered on Wednesday.

US forces seized Maduro and Flores from their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, in a dramatic, night-time raid on 3 January, and brought them to New York to face allegations of weapon and drug offences, which they deny.

Judge Alvin Hellerstein scheduled a pre-trial hearing for 17 November to hear motions from both parties.

Maduro's attorney Barry Pollack signalled that he will argue at trial that his client was protected by sovereign immunity, a legal principle shielding heads of state from prosecution.

The courtroom was packed with spectators, with some people lining up for hours for the chance to glimpse Maduro in person.

Before the hearing began, a court officer warned the public to remain seated and that that they "can't say anything to him."

Anyone who disobeyed decorum "might have some legal issues of your own," the officer warned.

The gallery mostly follows his instructions as Maduro and Flores were led into the chamber shortly after noon, but some murmured or inhaled breath as he walked past.

Maduro, who wore a beige jail uniform but was not handcuffed cuffed, gave the gallery a nod as he walked to his seat at the defence table.

He and Flores sat quietly, wearing headphones for translation while their attorneys conferred with the judge.

When it was time to leave, Maduro stood. He faced the public and gave a single wave of his hands, before disappearing into the bowels of the courthouse in the custody of US Marshalls.

Outside the courtroom, anti-war protesters condemned the US military operation that resulted in Maduro's capture, holding up signs that read "Free President Maduro," and decrying, in the words of one protester with a bullhorn, the "sham trial" taking place inside.

"The US is endeavouring to bring Venezuela, Latin America, and the Middle East under its thumb," said a speaker with the Anti-War Action Network.

Some Venezuelans, draped in the country's flag, supported the prosecution.

"Maduro is a criminal," said Wilmer Contreras, 53, who moved to the US about 30 years ago. "He's a part of the government, they destroyed my country completely."

Contreras said he "absolutely" supported the Trump administration's military capture of Maduro.

"What they did was something that we were expecting, and waiting for, for a long time. And when that happened, things changed in my country," he told the BBC.

News.title: Liverpool issue bans as £1.2m seized from ticket touts
News.content:
Liverpool have issued over 400 lifetime bans after more than Â£1.2m of assets relating to the illegal selling of tickets was seized by police.

The club worked with Merseyside Police to seize the assets from organised ticket touts.

The police operation focused on the laundering of criminal proceeds from illicit ticket sales and took place alongside the club's crackdown on ticket touting, both online and in the ground.

The club has since issued 432 lifetime bans to the guilty parties, as well as 115 indefinite suspensions.

Detective Chief Inspector Nick Suffield said: "This is a fantastic example of partnership working between ourselves and Liverpool Football Club for the good of the fans and the general public.

"We will always take action to protect genuine fans who fall victim to touts when all they are trying to do is simply purchase tickets to support their team."

From the assets seized, the money was split between Merseyside Police and the Home Office.

Last year, BBC Sport revealed Liverpool had shut down 145,000 ticket accounts over the previous two years as part of a crackdown on touting.

And last season alone, Liverpool analysed almost 700,000 ticket registrations, with 67,663 suspected fake accounts blocked or cancelled, and a further 121,379 accounts currently under investigation.

A further 3,847 tickets were cancelled for suspicious purchase activity in the 2025-26 season. They were put back on sale as general admission tickets, increasing the number available for genuine fans.

There was also a significant increase in targeted stops carried out on matchdays by the club, who prevented access to the turnstiles for accounts with suspicious activity.

These stops were carried out at Anfield â an average of 300 per home game â and at away games both in the Premier League and in Europe.

News.title: Burnham rebukes ministers after prisoner releases joke
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has rebuked some of his cabinet ministers after they were caught on camera sharing a joke about releasing prisoners.

In the footage, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting can be heard telling Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood that new Justice Secretary Alex Norris "wants to let them all out".

Streeting apologised for the remarks, which were first published by Metro journalist Craig Munro, after critics suggested he had been joking about the government's early prisoner release scheme.

Asked whether it was appropriate for his ministers to be joking about early release, Burnham told reporters: "No it's not, and certainly that's been acknowledged and apologies have been made."

The moment was captured on Tuesday, when broadcasters were invited to film members of Burnham's cabinet chatting ahead of their first meeting.

In the footage, Mahmood can be seen chatting with Streeting before breaking off to greet Norris, a former minister at the Home Office who was promoted to justice secretary by Burnham on Monday.

Streeting can then be heard joking to Mahmood that Norris is "the enemy now", to which she replies "no he's not".

Streeting goes on to say "he wants to let them all out", before Mahmood replies "You know who's boss!" and the pair share a laugh.

In a post on X, Streeting said he had been referencing a joke Theresa May used to make about Ken Clarke when the two of them occupied the same cabinet posts as Mahmood and Norris respectively in a Conservative government.

May has previously said that when she was home secretary, she would joke about Clarke: 'I locked 'em up and he let 'em out'".

He added: "I hope everyone can see there was no ill intent behind this ribbing of the new justice secretary.

"But I appreciate these are very serious issues and am sorry for any offence inadvertently caused by this moment of levity."

Mahmood released a similar comment, adding: "I appreciate this is an extremely serious issue and do not want anyone to mistake this moment of levity for a lack of serious intent."

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the pair of making light of the government's scheme to release some prisoners early to ease prison overcrowding, announced in 2024 when Mahmood was justice secretary.

"While Andy Burnham's cabinet are joking about letting criminals out of prison early, Conservatives are listening to victims and will continue to fight this disgusting policy," she wrote on X.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said it was "right" that Streeting had apologised.

"Those remarks don't reflect the seriousness with which all of them will approach matters relating to public safety and the prison system".

Shortly after coming to power in 2024, the Labour government announced emergency measures to release prisoners in England and Wales early to ease overcrowding, in a scheme that was later expanded.

Under the Sentencing Act, due to come into effect in September, some prisoners let out after serving a third of their sentence, while those who would previously have served two-thirds will instead be released after serving half of their sentence.

News.title: No helicopters to fight wildfires as 'crisis management' plans activated in Wales
News.content:
The Welsh government has activated "crisis management arrangements" due to the number of wildfires across the nation.

It comes amid criticism from residents over a lack of resources like helicopters to tackle the fires, some of which have been burning for days across north and south Wales.

The Welsh government said North Wales Fire and Rescue had received extra resources but aerial support was not available anywhere in the UK.

However, it said "urgent discussions are now underway both within Wales and at a UK level to identify how this can be resolved".

Meanwhile, firefighters are tackling a big blaze in south Wales for a third day, with the smoke travelling 30 miles (48km) away.

News.title: Over £100,000 raised for boy, 3, in croc attack
News.content:
More than Â£100,000 has been raised for a three-year-old boy who was attacked in a crocodile enclosure.

The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 18 June when he was attacked by at least one of the animals.

A fundraising page has raised Â£105,000 for the boy and his family after the three-year-old was taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital, where he has undergone seven surgeries.

Cambridgeshire Police arrested and bailed a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder after the incident.

News.title: Mid-air 10-person brawl halts easyJet   flight
News.content:
A mid-air brawl involving around 10 passengers forced a Liverpool-bound easyJet plane to fly back to Tenerife, according to air traffic control.

The captain decided to return to the Spanish island about 30 minutes after departure "due to the danger" the fight "posed to the safety of the flight", the air traffic controller said.

Police met flight EZY3352 when it touched down at Tenerife South airport on Tuesday evening, per the crew's request.

The 186-passenger aircraft then continued to Liverpool.

The air traffic controller said in its statement, originally written in Spanish: "Our full support goes out to the crews and passengers who are increasingly having to endure these situations."

EasyJet said the plane "returned to the airport and was met by police due to a group of passengers behaving disruptively.

News.title: Some food prices have fallen – but inflation expected to rise from here
News.content:
Food prices are rising at their slowest rate in nearly two years, as the cost of some staples such as margarine and sugar have gone down.

Supermarket price wars have helped drive down prices in the year to June, the industry says, as retailers work to tempt customers with summer deals.

Inflation in the UK overall has fallen to 2.6% in the year to June, down from 2.8% in the year to May, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), driven largely by lower fuel and food prices.

June's figure will be welcomed by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his government, but analysts warn the fall is temporary, as higher energy prices in July are expected to push inflation back up.

Lower fuel costs - particularly lower diesel prices - also pushed inflation down, with prices at the pump falling for the first time since the start of the war in the Middle East.

Clothing costs fell as well due to the summer sales, with many retailers offering larger discounts than last year.

News.title: 'No secrecy' over asylum camp decision, court told
News.content:
The Home Office did not act in secrecy over its decision to house asylum seekers at a former military training camp in East Sussex and engaged with relevant bodies beforehand and afterwards, the High Court has heard.

Community interest company Crowborough Shield is taking legal action over the government's use of Crowborough Training Camp to house up to 540 men.

The group claims the Home Office failed to exercise its powers with the openness required.

James Strachan KC, for the Home Office, said the Secretary of State engaged with the police, NHS and councils and once the decision was taken, a forum was established for people to address any issues.

News.title: Former Lloyd's of London boss's relationship breached rules, firm says
News.content:
Lloyd's of London's former boss's close relationship with another director breached compliance rules, the insurance market has said after an internal investigation.

Former chief executive John Neal and former corporate affairs director Rebekah Clement's relationship was "sufficiently close... that it could be viewed as creating a perceived conflict of interest", the firm said.

Lloyd's said the pair breached compliance rules by not disclosing their relationship but found no conclusive evidence they had a romantic relationship while at Lloyd's.

Neal said all parties can now move on. Clement's lawyer said she is considering legal action.

"Rebekah is hugely disappointed with Lloyd's conduct over the course of this investigation, the nature and length of which have caused her unnecessary stress and significant reputational damage relative to its 'findings'," Clement's lawyer added.

"She is not surprised that Lloyd's found no evidence of an inappropriate relationship with John Neal, nor any evidence of any failings in her promotion. She also co-operated with the investigation throughout.

"Yet, Lloyd's has still chosen to find against Rebekah, on the pretext of 'perception', the source of which was rumour, gossip and innuendo."

Neal said: "I am pleased, but not at all surprised, that the investigation found there was no inappropriate relationship.

"I would have hoped less time and resource had been spent in reaching a conclusion on the central question that was, in truth, never in doubt.

"I am disappointed with the other findings and do not accept them."

Lloyd's said on Wednesday that it first received "certain whistleblowing reports" in November 2023 but that it didn't act on them.

It said its chairman Sir Charles Roxburgh judged this to be a governance failure and informed the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) about it in October 2025.

Lloyd's said it could not share the nature of these allegations or the identities of the people involved.

In November 2025, Lloyd's said Sir Charles became aware of "new information related to an alleged personal relationship" between Neal and Clement and "immediately launched an expanded investigation into the matter".

Lloyd's said its investigation was hampered by the fact that Neal and Clement had both left the company and refused to answer questions, but Lloyd's said it interviewed nearly 40 witnesses in its probe.

It added that it has kept the FCA informed throughout the process.

Sir Charles said on Wednesday: "Based on the findings of this investigation, we have concluded that the conduct of the former chief executive fell significantly below the standards expected of him."

He added the investigation "established serious failings in the governance standards and in following processes, most worryingly in the handling of whistleblowing reports. These were serious failures that should never have been allowed to happen."

Lloyd's history as a City institution stretches back well over 300 years, with its first recorded mention appearing in 1688.

News.title: Glasgow School of Art cannot afford to restore fire-hit Mackintosh building
News.content:
Glasgow School of Art says it cannot fully restore the city's iconic Mackintosh Building to its former state without additional financial support.

The art school previously insisted it was committed to a faithful reinstatement of the building, which was designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh but wrecked by two fires in 2014 and 2018.

However it now says "financial clarity", provided by an insurance settlement regarding the 2018 blaze, has shown it "cannot take forward the faithful reinstatement on its own."

Instead it suggests the building has potential to be an anchor for a "creative and cultural production innovation district".

But this claim that has attracted scorn from figures in the art world.

Green groups and opposition politicians have criticised the government over its decision to fund its new £500m policy capping bus fares in England at £2 using the climate aid budget.

The new transport policy, which was announced today, is set to reverse an cap increase to £3 that was put in place by Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves in 2024, and is being billed as a landmark measure intended to tackle the cost of living crisis .

Around £400m of the cost is set to come from switching government investment in international climate finance from grants to loans, with the rest from savings in the budget of the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero and about £50m from Department for Transport.

Mohamed Adow, director of Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa, was among those criticising the funding move, saying: "Balancing the books on the backs of the world's poorest and most vulnerable people is the wrong choice.

“ Climate finance was never meant to be a pot of money that governments raid when they need to pay for domestic spending. It is part of the UK's responsibility to help countries that have contributed least to the climate crisis but are suffering its worst impacts.”

Liberal Democrat MP Monica Harding added that while it is “right to be cutting bus fares”, she believes that Burnham’s approach is “going to further undermine the UK’s standing as a reliable global partner”.

Green MP Ellie Chowns added: “Reducing bus fares is welcome, but it is morally wrong to do so by loading more debt onto some of the poorest countries that have contributed least to the climate crisis and are experiencing some of its most severe consequences.”

The new funding announcement comes after the government already slashed the amount of aid it is set to provide to climate projects as part of its broader programme of aid cuts , from £11.6bn over the past five years (average £2.3bn per year) to £6bn over the next three (average £2bn per year).

Others said switching funding from grants to loans risks exacerbating the debt crises that many developing countries are currently struggling with following global shocks including Covid-19 and the impact of Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Many charities have in recent months been highly critical of the UK government for not doing enough to assist indebted developing countries.

“Tackling the cost of living crisis and deepening household debt in the UK should not be paid for by piling more debt onto people in lower-income countries like Malawi and Zambia,” said Heidi Chow, executive director of pressure group Debt Justice

“This is a slap in the face to countries already facing the double catastrophe of an escalating debt crisis and the climate emergency ,” she added.

Romily Greenhill, CEO of development charity network Bond, said that it is “disappointing that the new Prime Minister is picking up where the previous one left off” by continuing to “raid the diminished UK aid budget” to tackle the cost of living crisis.

In response to the concerns raised by green groups, a government spokesperson said: “We are committed to spending 0.3 per cent [of Gross National Income] on Official Development Assistance.

“Switching a small proportion of that spending from grants to loans give us more flexible ways to tackle the climate crisis while making the best use of taxpayers’ money.”

News.title: Dog found 30 miles from home is reunited with owners after going missing for 10 days
News.content:
A seven-year-old Australian shepherd dog named Fig was reunited with her owners after being missing for 10 days.

The canine fled after being startled by July 4th fireworks. Owner Katie Cassaday and her family spent a week posting flyers and searching for her without success.

But after filing a missing dog report with Tulare County Sheriff’s Department, Fig was spotted nearly 30 miles from her California home.

The sheriff’s department posted a bodycam video showing an officer reuniting Fig with her family on July 15th.

William Shatner has revealed that he was dealing with stage 4 cancer at the same time as his daughter, Melanie Shatner Gretsch.

The 95-year-old Canadian actor told People in an interview published Wednesday that Gretsch, 61, was diagnosed with stage 4 breast cancer in 2022 after finding a lump in her breast.

Shatner revealed that about a year later, in June 2023, he was diagnosed with stage 4 melanoma, a serious form of skin cancer, that had spread to his lungs and brain.

“I remember vividly thinking, ‘I don’t have the strength to take care of myself and lose my father at the same time,’” Gretsch, the youngest daughter of Shatner and first wife Gloria Rand, told the outlet.

The father-daughter duo were both declared cancer-free by late 2024.

open image in gallery William Shatner has revealed he is cancer-free after being diagnosed with stage 4 melanoma ( AFP/Getty )

Shatner said: “We got the perfect doctors for her cancer and my cancer.”

In the year and a half after her diagnosis, Gretsch — who has two children with husband Joel Gretsch— said she underwent multiple rounds of chemotherapy, a double mastectomy and 30 radiation therapy treatments.

Gretsch said her father offered to help her financially during her treatment, saying: “I do not want you to worry. Just send me the bills.”

“Then you made me laugh so hard when I was still going to the doctor a year later,” she said to the Star Trek actor, according to People. “You said, ‘You’ve got to get well. We’re going to be in the poorhouse!’”

However, when she was nearly done with her treatments, her father found a lump in his cheek that turned out to be a tumor. He had surgery to remove it and underwent two years of immunotherapy to fight the cancer.

open image in gallery Melanie Shatner, pictured here in 2006, married actor Joel Gretsch in 1999 ( Getty )

Shatner previously opened up about the fear he felt when he was diagnosed. During a 2024 keynote presentation at the American Academy of Dermatology Annual Meeting, he recalled: “I said, ‘Stage 4?’ And someone in the room said, ‘Sorry.’ I said, ‘What are you sorry about?’ It was like, ‘Better pack your things.’ That person who said ‘sorry,’ that was very sad, like you are going to die. And I was. They said if this [treatment] they used did not work, I had about 5 months.”

The two-time Emmy winner told People that his cancer diagnosis made him more grateful for the little things in his life.

“It’s easy for us in this lovely home to say, ‘Make your life meaningful.’ It’s much more difficult to be poverty-stricken and wonder how you’re going to get through it. I’ve been there,” Shatner told the outlet.

“But it’s also possible to endure that and be aware of the beauty around you,” he said.

Charles Gaines, the acclaimed author whose seminal work and documentary Pumping Iron propelled professional bodybuilding into the mainstream and introduced the world to Arnold Schwarzenegger, has died at 84.

His daughter, Greta Gaines, confirmed his passing Tuesday, though she did not disclose a cause. In a heartfelt tribute, she wrote: "You always marched to your own drummer and inspired everyone around you to do the same. Follow that bliss, catch that fish and kiss those lips while you can because my father was the live life to the fullest kinda guy."

Gaines collaborated with George Butler on Pumping Iron: The Art and Sport of Bodybuilding, a book that subsequently led to the creation of the influential 1977 documentary, for which both men penned the script. In the introduction to their 1974 book, Gaines described it as "a sort of respectful report from the interior of an interesting, colorful and heretofore ignored region of American life."

He later admitted in a 2022 edition that neither author anticipated widespread interest, noting that Schwarzenegger almost single-handedly "brought bodybuilding out of the shadows it had languished in since its earliest days in America and into the limelight."

Schwarzenegger, a seven-time Mr. Olympia and five-time Mr. Universe champion featured flexing on the cover of Pumping Iron, leveraged this newfound attention into a remarkable career. He transitioned from blockbuster films like The Terminator, True Lies, Twins, and Predator to politics, serving as California’s governor from 2003 to 2011.

open image in gallery Arnold Schwarzenegger during the 38th Cannes film festival where he presented Pumping Iron , a documentary that spread his fame beyond bodybuilding circles ( AFP via Getty Images )

Gaines himself had a lifelong connection to bodybuilding, having started lifting weights at 16. Pumping Iron originated as a 1972 Sports Illustrated article covering a Mr. East Coast bodybuilding contest.

He famously wrote, "If we felt at times a little like 19th century explorers, it was because we found bodybuilding to be as primeval and unmapped as parts of Labrador. Nobody, we discovered, had been back into it to send out a report on what it was like."

The documentary famously chronicled the rivalry between Schwarzenegger and fellow bodybuilder Lou Ferrigno, who later starred in The Incredible Hulk, during their quest for the Mr. Olympia title.

A prolific writer, Gaines published numerous books, including Waters Far and Near: Tales of Angling Adventure and Misadventure Around the World and the novels Stay Hungry, Dangler, and Survival Games. Stay Hungry was adapted into a film starring Jeff Bridges, providing Schwarzenegger with his inaugural movie role.

Schwarzenegger shared his condolences on Instagram, stating: "He climbed mountains, trekked across ice, fished, and hunted on almost every continent, writing about every adventure in a way that captured people’s hearts and minds. He was interested in everything — and his interest was contagious. I’m lucky that he was always looking for new frontiers, because that’s how he found me and our niche sport of bodybuilding."

Gaines, who was raised in Alabama, earned a bachelor's degree from Birmingham-Southern College and a Master of Fine Arts in writing from the University of Iowa. He is survived by his wife, artist Patricia Ellisor Gaines, and his three children, Greta, Latham, and Shelby Gaines.

Tom Holland has revealed he felt "intimidated" when he first met renowned director Sir Christopher Nolan.

The 30-year-old actor is set to portray Telemachus in Nolan’s much-anticipated adaptation of Homer’s ancient Greek epic, The Odyssey.

The film will follow Odysseus, played by Matt Damon, the Greek king of Ithaca, as he makes his arduous 10-year journey home after the Trojan War.

Holland is also preparing to reprise his iconic role as Spider-Man in Brand New Day, which is due for release later this month.

Questioned on how he reacted to being asked if he would like to be in the film, on the Dish From Waitrose podcast, Holland said: “I mean, obviously the first word out of your mouth is ‘yes’.

Holland stars in the film alongside Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Lupita Nyong’o, Samantha Morton, Zendaya and Charlize Theron ( Universal Pictures )

“I was really intimidated to meet him, but he’s a very disarming person, he’s really kind, he’s really personable, and he was really open about the ambition of what he wanted to try and do.

“And I love film, I love making movies, I love watching movies, and I was just excited as a fan of cinema to hear what he was planning on doing, and then to get the chance to be in it was just… I’m still to this day kind of pinching myself.

“Knowing that I’m going to his premiere tonight is exciting enough, and now knowing that like I’m in it, I mean, it’s crazy to me still.”

He said that the 55-year-old director had no phone and as a result he was called in to meet him rather than by Sir Christopher himself.

Holland added: “You come and sit down with him, and for a long time we just chatted as just two people, about film, and then he kind of dropped the mic and said, ‘the movie I want to make is The Odyssey’.

“And then immediately in my head trying to remember what The Odyssey was about, trying to seem intelligent… but you know it was amazing, he pitched me the story, he told me the role.

“I took the script home that night and read it, and was absolutely floored by his ability to adapt something that’s so massive, I think he’s so celebrated as a director, he’s often overlooked as a writer.”

The actor called The Odyssey, which is the first film to have been shot entirely with Imax film cameras, “probably the biggest movie that has ever been made”.

The film also stars Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Lupita Nyong’o, Samantha Morton, Zendaya and Charlize Theron, and is in cinemas now.

The full interview can be heard on the Dish From Waitrose podcast which is available on all major podcast providers.

Conservative political commentator Bill O’Reilly recommended that his old friend President Donald Trump “take the next month off” and “relax a little bit,” perhaps with golfing.

After discussing several of Trump’s current woes, including the recent pushback against lethal Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations and disputes with broadcast networks not airing Trump’s recent speech, O’Reilly offered the president a piece of advice on his show “No Spin News.”

“I’ve noticed that he’s hunching over a little bit, and that’s normal. You get older, every malady in the world is going to visit you,” O’Reilly said Tuesday, of the 80-year-old president who he described as his friend for decades.

“So my advice to Donald Trump is to take the next month off, if you can, get into an environment where you like – golf. And relax a little bit,” O’Reilly added.

Though the war in Iran is ongoing, O’Reilly, 76, suggested Trump could continue to prioritize negotiations by using his phone or the people on his team.

open image in gallery Conservative commentator Bill O'Reilly said the president appeared 'hunched' and could use a break from leading the United States ( Bill O'Reilly, No Spin News / YouTube )

“You need a breather,” the former Fox News host said.

Presidents can, and have, taken vacations while in office, but they cannot be entirely unplugged from their job.

Trump is known to take weekend trips to his golf clubs, often in Florida or New Jersey, which can function as small getaways. An online tracker that records each time the president spends a day golfing indicates the president has spent 116 days of his 549 days in office golfing.

Though some of those golf outings are work-related.

During his first term, Trump was adamant that his time spent away from the White House was a “working vacation,” even while spending more than two weeks at his golf club located in Bedminster, New Jersey.

The president’s team often boasts about how often Trump is working, consistently claiming the president does not sleep very much and spends a lot of time making calls.

open image in gallery Trump is known to take weekend trips to go golfing, but O’Reilly is calling for longer than that ( AFP/Getty )

But the anecdotes offer little solace to critics who point out the president’s voice is hoarse during speeches, appears to fall asleep during meetings or press conferences, has bruised hands from consistent aspirin use and stumbles over words.

Though Trump shows signs of aging, he often brushes off concerns about his mental and physical acuity and states he is in great shape and feels younger than he is.

Tucker Carlson, a prominent conservative podcaster and former ally to Trump, told the New York Times in June that Trump is “really uncomfortable” with aging.

The White House has consistently defended Trump, comparing his “sharpness, unmatched energy and historic accessibility” with his predecessor, former President Joe Biden. They’ve reiterated that Trump is in good health.

But O’Reilly, who said he’s known Trump for 35 years, seems to think his friend could use a break.

“We wish the best for not only President Trump but all the presidents, even Joe Biden, Barack Obama, Jimmy Carter,” O’Reilly said Tuesday.

Argentina fly half Tomas Albornoz has been charged with misconduct and faces a disciplinary hearing after “remonstrating with match officials” follow his side’s defeat to England in Santiago del Estero.

Albornoz was denied a chance to kick for a potential draw after a last-minute try was ruled out by referee Angus Gardner in consultation with television match official (TMO) Brett Cronan.

The officials ruled that Bautista Delguy had grounded the ball simultaneously on the try-line and corner flag, and thus not scored, as England held on for a 31-24 victory.

Albornoz appeared to approach Gardner and his assistants aggressively thereafter, and has now been charged by World Rugby under its Match Official Abuse Sanction Process,

The details of his disciplinary hearing will be released in due course.

“The Match Official Abuse Sanction Process was introduced to complement Regulation 18 and provide a clearer and more consistent framework for addressing public criticism of match officials, particularly where such comments may contribute to wider online abuse,” World Rugby explained in a statement.

“Developed by a cross-game working group including competition owner, match official playing and coaching representation and championed by Union CEOs, the process reflects a unified commitment to support and protect match officials.”

Argentina were disappointed that Delguy’s try was chalked off, and that no penalty try was awarded for an apparent high tackle by Noah Caluori.

Head coach Felipe Contepomi later accused the visitors of showing a “lack of respect” after abruptly leaving his press conference with England playing celebratory music nearby.

News.title: Inflation fall a ‘false dawn’, Burnham warned
News.content:
Falling inflation is a “false dawn” for Andy Burnham, economists warned after the pace of price rises slowed in June.

The consumer prices index (CPI) fell from 2.8pc in May to 2.6pc last month, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), beating economists’ expectations of a drop to 2.7pc to mark the lowest rate in 15 months.

Lower petrol and diesel prices drove the slowdown amid a short-lived peace deal between the US and Iran, while price pressures from chocolate, oils and fats, dairy and meat also weakened.

However, economists warned a rise in household energy bills in July may already have pushed inflation back up above 3pc.

Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants, said: “June’s slowdown is a false dawn as it may have already been reversed this month with higher energy bills, following Ofgem’s energy price cap rise, likely to have lifted inflation above 3pc.”

July’s 13pc increase in the energy price cap has pushed typical annual bills to around £1,862, while renewed fighting between the US and Iran has reignited concerns over oil and gas supplies.

Mr Thiru said elevated inflation would create a fresh headache for John Healey, the newly appointed Chancellor, by squeezing household budgets, raising government borrowing costs and limiting his room for tax cuts or spending increases.

Charlotte O’Leary, at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said: “June’s peace deal and the subsequent reduction in oil and gas prices helped cool consumer price inflation. This will be a welcome figure to start the new Prime Minister’s premiership, but the honeymoon period will be short-lived.”

The Bank of England will also be watching closely as it weighs further interest rate cuts, though economists warned renewed instability in the Middle East and higher energy bills could keep inflation close to 3pc for the rest of the year.

Mr Healey said: “Falling inflation is news families want to hear, but there is much more to do to give people the breathing space they need.”

News.title: Russia destroys Ukraine HIV warehouse
News.content:
A Russian missile strike has destroyed $2.6m (£1.9m) worth of HIV prevention supplies in Ukraine, according to an international aid group.

The Alliance for Public Health said the attack on Sunday night near Kyiv hit a warehouse holding 62 million prevention items earmarked for Ukraine’s harm reduction programmes next year. It includes syringes, needles, alcohol wipes, and condoms intended to support more than 300,000 people.

“This is not just another strike. It is an attack on 300,000 Ukrainians who depend on HIV prevention services and on their fundamental right to health,” said Andriy Klepikov, executive director of the Alliance for Public Health.

Efforts to prevent the spread of HIV rely heavily on harm reduction programmes that supply sterile syringes and needles to people who inject drugs, alongside condoms and other supplies that help curb sexual transmission.

Mr Klepikov said the destruction of the warehouse would not immediately disrupt services, because his organisation had moved its supplies for the rest of the year out of central storage and into regional distribution centres several weeks ago as part of contingency planning.

“Russia failed,” he said, adding that the Alliance had notified international partners and appealed for urgent support to rebuild next year’s inventory.

News.title: Private sector pay suffers worst growth since Covid
News.content:
Private sector wages are growing at their slowest pace since the pandemic, piling pressure on Andy Burnham as he enters Downing Street facing a fragile economy and strained public finances.

Salaries rose by 2.9pc in the three months to May, the first time growth has dipped below 3pc since October 2020 and only narrowly ahead of inflation at 2.8pc.

The slowdown was most acute in key industries, with wages in finance and business services up just 2.3pc, manufacturing at 2.5pc and construction earnings falling by 0.2pc over the year.

In contrast, public sector pay accelerated to 5.5pc after striking workers secured higher settlements, widening the gap between state and private sectors.

The cooling labour market came as borrowing overshot official forecasts, leaving John Healey, the new Chancellor, with a £2.7bn gap against expectations.

The Government borrowed £57.6bn between April and June – less than a year earlier but still ahead of projections – pushing public debt to nearly £3tn, or 94.9pc of GDP.

Mr Healey said: “The Prime Minister and I have talked about how we will work in lockstep to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty and how we’ll make life more affordable for working people right across the UK.”

However, Sir Mel Stride, the shadow business secretary, said: “If Andy Burnham and John Healey are really serious about the future of our economy then they must get borrowing under control.”

News.title: Scammers stole $114 billion as Southeast Asia’s crime gangs go corporate
News.content:
Scam gangs stole up to $114 billion from people in Asia-Pacific alone in 2025, the UN has warned, as crime syndicates rapidly professionalise their tactics to evade law enforcement in Southeast Asia.

By way of comparison, the sum dwarfs the $85 billion the UK spends each year on defence.

The Asia-Pacific region has emerged as an epicentre for massive cyber fraud operations since the Covid pandemic. Scammers – some willingly, others under duress – are now stealing billions from internet users across the world via fake romance and cryptocurrency investment schemes.

In 2025, these fraud operations stole between $88.3 and $114.1bn from just people across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, according to a report on Tuesday from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

Those figures are triple the estimated losses in 2023, between $18 and $37bn, and don’t account for victims in Europe or the US.

The scam centres – which began in fortified compounds but are now increasingly housed in innocuous office blocks and villas – are found across the region, but have especially exploited power vacuums caused by war, corruption and weak governance in Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos.

Although the scammers initially targeted people in China, they have dramatically expanded their ambitions. The UNODC said people from at least 80 countries and territories had been identified in compounds, with recruiters seeking people from outside Asia as they look to expand new markets.

News.title: UK borrowing costs rise at fastest pace in G7
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs rose at the fastest pace in the G7 after Andy Burnham said he would take a “flexible” approach to the UK’s fiscal rules.

In his maiden speech as prime minister, Mr Burnham on Monday signalled he could bend the rules underpinning Britain’s finances, spooking financial markets fearful of higher government spending.

UK gilts – a benchmark for how much the Government pays on its debt – saw yields rise 0.08 percentage points to an eight-week high of 5.03pc for the 10-year bond. Thirty-year gilts also pushed higher.

The rise was the fastest in the G7, excluding Japan, whose markets are closed for a national holiday.

After markets closed on Monday, Mr Burnham surprised the City by picking John Healey as his next Chancellor.

Mr Healey, who quit over defence funding rising too slowly, will now be tasked with finding billions of pounds in Britain’s stretched public finances.

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, had widely been expected for the role. Ed Miliband, the former Energy Secretary, was also in contention.

Mr Healey will replace Rachel Reeves, who resigned on Monday.

The appointment of Mr Healey, a veteran of the Blair-Brown government, may calm fears in the City after Mr Burnham pledged to stretch the fiscal rules by using “flexibility” within them.

Speaking in Downing Street, Mr Burnham said: “I’ve said we’ll stick to the fiscal rules, and by that I mean the existing fiscal rules, and use obviously any flexibility within them.”

James Athey, a fund manager at Marlborough, said: “It’s not a good start because bandying around the words fiscal rules seems to be believed within government circles to be a sufficient condition to get financial markets on side, and that just misunderstands an element of the problem.”

He added that investors were watching closely for any signs that the Government will increase borrowing.

Matt Amis, investment director at Aberdeen, said Mr Burnham’s comments had “got the markets’ attention.”

He said “It just shows this week in particular the language from the Burnham administration, the new chancellor, is going to be key here. The gilt market is on edge.”

Mr Burnham, who has become the UK’s seventh prime minister in just a decade, has inherited a troubled economy as businesses grapple with low confidence and strained public finances.

Monday’s comment suggests the new prime minister will use measures to raise borrowing while keeping the additional sums off the Government’s book.

The Resolution Foundation, a think tank, said he could do this by expanding the remit of institutions like the National Wealth Fund, an arms-length government investment vehicle.

His plan to use “flexibility” in the fiscal rules comes after Ms Reeves altered the main indicator of government debt in 2024.

She tweaked the primary measure of the UK’s debt to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities, meaning that when public financial institutions borrow to invest in a private business it does not count towards the government’s fiscal rules.

However, the think tank warned that boosting the financial capacity of public financial institutions like the National Wealth Fund by £16bn would cost around £400 million a year in debt interest.

Helen Miller, director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that challenging public finances will mean Mr Burnham will be forced to make tough choices on spending.

She said: “While chancellors come and go, the underlying fiscal constraints remain the same. Public debt, borrowing and debt-interest costs are all high. One in every £12 the government spends currently goes on debt interest.”

Higher borrowing costs threaten to increase the Government’s debt interest bill, which is already forecast to hit £111.2bn for the financial year - equivalent to 8.3pc of public spending.

Mr Burnham said he would announce a set of measures on Tuesday to give households “breathing space” to help with the cost of living.

“I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them,” he said.

“We will help more young people into education... and we will build more council homes. That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.”

Mr Amis said: “Tomorrow we’re getting some cost of living news. [Burnham] said he was going to state where that funding’s come from. I think that’s key, any unfunded spending from here would get the market’s attention.”

News.title: India approves first dengue vaccine as cases surge in South Asia
News.content:
India has approved its first dengue vaccine as cases of the mosquito-borne disease surge in South Asia.

Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical’s dengue vaccine QDENGA has been approved by India’s drug regulator, the Centre Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).

The global threat posed by dengue has been rising for years, as climate change, urbanisation and international travel aid the spread of the mosquitoes that transmit it.

The approval comes as hospitals across South Asia grapple with a surge in dengue infections.

In Sri Lanka, health authorities reported 2,652 new cases on Sunday alone, taking the total to 76,044 dengue cases so far this year. At least 53 people have died.

Bangladesh is also suffering a major outbreak with over 9,000 cases and 30 deaths that has piled pressure on its health system even as it battles a measles epidemic.

Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.

Its symptoms include fever, severe muscle pain, and in severe cases, shock and internal bleeding that can be fatal.

Although mortality is relatively low, outbreaks place a substantial burden on health systems.

Takeda’s QDENGA jab is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It can be given regardless of previous dengue infections.

“The approval comes at a critical time for public health, as reported dengue cases in India have increased 11-fold in the past two decades,” the company said in a statement.

News.title: Burnham’s plan to restore UK aid spending
News.content:
Andy Burnham is planning to reverse the cuts to Britain’s aid budget made by his predecessors Sir Keir Starmer and Rishi Sunak, according to reports.

A roadmap for returning the UK to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross National Income (GNI) on international aid will be drawn up as part of a major shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), The Independent reported.

Ed Miliband is set to be named Foreign Secretary and put in charge of overhauling Britain’s international development aims, as well as prioritising climate goals, senior Labour sources said.

The aid spending plan was absent from Mr Burnham’s brief first speech as Prime Minister, in which he pledged to end rough sleeping and bring down the welfare bill in order to fund defence and council housing.

But it follows anger within the Labour Party over what was seen as a broken manifesto promise, when Sir Keir and Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor, slashed aid spending to 0.3 per cent of GNI.

Senior Labour MPs have been lobbying for a return to the 0.7 per cent commitment, a target first established by the United Nations in the 1970s.

It has since become a key yardstick for international efforts to reduce poverty and tackle major health issues like the HIV/AIDS epidemic, vaccine access, and maternal mortality in poor countries.

Sports.title: Man Utd plot Aurelien Tchouameni transfer despite rejecting Real Madrid star
Sports.content:
Man Utd plot Aurelien Tchouameni transfer despite rejecting Real Madrid star

Manchester United have made moves as they look to sign Real Madrid star Aurelien Tchouameni even if reports claim the midfielder has signed a new deal with Los Blancos

View 2 Images Aurelien Tchouameni has been linked with a move to Manchester (Image: Getty Images)

Manchester United have enquired about Real Madrid star Aurelien Tchouameni despite reports that the Frenchman has signed a new deal in Spain.

‌



The Red Devils remain in the market for midfield additions despite already bringing in Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans from Chelsea and Aston Villa respectively. Tchouameni would be their most blockbuster signing if they could get a deal of the line.

‌



The 26-year-old will have some down time after the World Cup before reporting for pre-season, but new Real boss Jose Mourinho has no interest in selling.

‌



Tchouameni is under contract at the Bernabeu until 2028, but there is speculation suggesting he's agreed a new contract to 2031, although nothing has been announced. Nevertheless The Sun claims those on the red side of Manchester have made moves as they bid to sign the ex-Monaco man.

Liverpool confident of beating Arsenal to £100m star as they move on second winger READ MORE :

Tchouameni is a specialist defensive midfielder and United are in the market for a player of that ilk to replace Casemiro, who was allowed to leave following the expiry of his contract.

United's midfield has been their priority this summer with Kobbie Mainoo among the only names who was present last year guaranteed to be part of Michael Carrick's plans. Manuel Ugarte's future is unclear but his injury could make him difficult to sell.

‌



The club enjoyed huge success with their recruitment 12 months ago, when attack was their priority. They went after proven Premier League quality in Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha, who both proved to be hits. Tielemans and Santos also know the league - with Tchouameni a potential overseas buy.

View 2 Images Youri Tielemans joined Man Utd earlier this summer (Image: Getty Images)

United were offered the chance to sign Tchouameni back in 2021 when he was still on Monaco's books, but did not have the budget for a midfielder. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, who was in charge at Old Trafford at the time, was keen on recruiting a young midfielder and had Declan Rice as his favoured target.

Article continues below

Talk of Real cashing in on Tchouameni has ramped up since the World Cup, where Rodri was named the tournament's best player after Spain claimed glory. The Manchester City midfielder was the Ballon d'Or winner only two years ago and he's been heavily linked with a move to the Bernabeu.

Sports.title: Morgan Rogers announcement shows Chelsea have already changed under Xabi Alonso
Sports.content:
Morgan Rogers announcement shows Chelsea have already changed under Xabi Alonso

The £117million acquisition of the England midfielder shows a shift in Chelsea's transfer policy that bodes well for the prospect of a realistic title challenge next season

View 3 Images Xabi Alonso was hugely influential in Morgan Rogers' decision to join Chelsea (Image: Chelsea FC via Getty Images)

It is a simple photograph but one that should fire up optimism in every Chelsea fan out there, with Xabi Alonso and Morgan Rogers lighting up the room with their smiles. Alonso and Rogers - not a sporting director in sight.

‌



So many of the myriad signings made during this ownership’s tenure have seemed like business enterprises rather than footballing enterprises. So many have seemed like projects dreamt up by the moneymen and agents, having nothing to do with the man who needs to put a decent team out on the pitch.

‌



But the £117million acquisition of Rogers seems like a pure footballing move, driven by Alonso, who is the manager AND the coach. If they tempt John Stones to Stamford Bridge, it will be a pure footballing move, just as it will be if they buy Crystal Palace defender Maxence Lacroix.

‌



This is Alonso making his mark. The only thing you can see Rogers doing under the guidance of Alonso - one of the most accomplished midfielders the Premier League has seen - is flourishing.

Can Argentina Premier League players have visas revoked after World Cup uproar? READ MORE :

It might well have been a fairly crude psychological ploy to provoke a reaction from the Real Madrid man but there was a time when Thomas Tuchel preferred Rogers to Jude Bellingham. And Rogers never let Tuchel down. Rogers never let England down.

Rogers turns 24 on Sunday and has plenty of developing to do, especially now he will be in harness with great friend, Cole Palmer. Rogers’ words on Palmer were more reasons for supporter optimism.

‌



“He is non-stop ringing my phone, texting me, and I can’t wait. I think that’s probably the most special thing, playing with one of your best friends and being around him every day. It’s something I’m really excited about.”

View 3 Images Morgan Rogers shares a goal celebration with his great friend Cole Palmer (Image: Neville Williams/Aston Villa FC via Getty Images)

And something Chelsea fans should be very excited about, not least for the fact that it underlines Palmer’s commitment to the club, which was not always taken for granted by sections of the fanbase.

‌



Chelsea are also one of the clubs bidding for the services of Bournemouth’s Alex Scott, who would be a hugely dependable replacement for Enzo Fernandez if they can get a nine-figure fee for the Argentinian.

Rogers, possibly Stones, possibly Scott - these are established Premier League performers. Obviously, the fee for Rogers is on the big side, to say the least. But Rogers brings a versatility that Alonso will love.

If Alonso uses the back-three system that served him so well at Bayer Leverkusen, there could be the mouthwatering prospect of Palmer and Rogers lining up as dual number 10s. In 55 appearances for Aston Villa last season, Rogers contributed 14 goals and 12 assists.

‌



View 3 Images Chelsea are interested in signing free agent John Stones (Image: CameraSport via Getty Images)

Across his last two seasons, Rogers has 18 Premier League goals and 16 Premier League assists. Those are very good numbers.

A lucrative seven-year deal obviously had a lot to do with Rogers’ choice of club but it is also clear that working with the manager had something to do with it. There can be no doubt Alonso is a draw-card for potential signings and knowing Chelsea, there will be more of those this summer.

Article continues below

There will also be plenty of outgoings, all of whom will be shipped out with Alonso’s blessing. In other words, it will be good, conventional transfer market business for a good, conventional manager.

He has not managed a game yet but the immediate impact of Alonso’s arrival has been to make a dysfunctional club look like a functional challenger once again. How Alonso and Chelsea actually perform in terms of performance and results remains to be seen but it will be one of the Premier League’s more compelling narratives, that is for sure.

Sports.title: Aston Villa are inviting a nightmare to their door with ludicrous Alejandro Garnacho transfer
Sports.content:
Aston Villa are inviting a nightmare to their door with ludicrous Alejandro Garnacho transfer

Aston Villa have sold Morgan Rogers to Chelsea in a record-breaking £117million transfer and as they look to bring in players of their own have turned to Alejandro Garnacho

View 2 Images Unai Emery led Aston Villa into the Champions League but has lost key players this summer (Image: 2026 Getty Images)

Aston Villa are about to swing violently from the sublime to the ridiculous. With a decision so bizarre, it feels akin to parking a Robin Reliant where a Ferrari has just been.

‌



Perhaps Unai Emery thinks he can be the manager to release the handbreak belonging to Alejandro Garnacho. What other reason could there be for the Villa manager to think there is some logic to replacing Morgan Rogers with Garnacho?

‌



But the real mistake Emery has made is convincing himself Garnacho is a good footballer in the first place.

‌



There were several reasons Garnacho failed to make the Argentina squad for this summer's World Cup. These included his attitude in training, approach to the game in general and an unhealthy obsession with social media. But the one which stuck out like a sore thumb, was also the one which saw Lionel Messi raise concerns about how disruptive Garnacho is capable of being in a squad and its dressing room.

In short, Emery has invited a nightmare to his own doorstep.

‌



Emery has earned a reputation for reviving lost causes in the past. The likes of Marcus Rashford and Marco Asensio spring to mind.

But the Spaniard has bitten off more than he can chew, this time.

When Chelsea agreed to hand over £40m to Manchester United for Garnacho last summer, Sir Jim Ratcliffe was said to be doing a dance of delight around the swimming pool of his mansion on the outskirts of Monaco. The United co-owner must have felt like popping an expensive bottle of the finest French champagne.

‌



He had rid his club of a footballer who had helped inject poison into the Old Trafford dressing room. Someone who personified United's previous indulgences with spoiled brats. A footballer with the ego of Eric Cantona, but the footballing talent of Eric Morecambe.

Villa supporters won't be laughing though. In fact, no-one associated with the club should be.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



View 2 Images Alejandro Garnacho has no future at Chelsea under Xabi Alonso (Image: John Walton/PA Wire)

Garnacho is someone who tries to write cheques his abilities cannot cash. The bright lights of London came calling, but Garnacho remained glued to the dimmer switch.

In a combined 117 league appearances for both United and Chelsea, Garnacho has scored the sum total of 17 goals.

‌



When Chelsea made the mind-boggling decision to sign Garnacho, United's gain was their loss. It summed up the London club's obsession with disfunction and arrogance.

And now, it seems, Emery is about to fall into the same trap.

He cannot seem to see what the rest of football can. The game is about the company you keep, and Emery is about to invite a troublemaker into his ranks. Because the only thing Garnacho is good at is getting managers the sack.
