World.title: Appetite for reflection
World.content:
Paul Taylor of Winston Hills doesn’t mind a bit of mobile fare when he says: “I’ve only just noticed that the badge on newer models of BYD appears as CYE when the car approaches in the rear-view mirror. I did wonder about any subliminal messaging but can only conclude that it may be a traditionally formatted attempt to cash in on the burgeoning fast food delivery car market. Perhaps it should be read as Express Yum Cha.”

“I can sympathise with Jack Dikian’s childhood recollections of watching Play School (C8) and his disappointment in choosing the incorrect window,” says Viv Munter of Tumbi Umbi. “During the ’70s, I recall watching Romper Room and waiting with bated breath for Miss Helena to acknowledge my name when she peered through the magic mirror. Disappointingly, she could never see me.”

“Hey, Jim Dewar. As one of your old fossils (C8), I’m sure that there must be someone, somewhere, that would complain about my demise,” hopes Robert Hosking of Paddington. “Meanwhile, I am seeking bids from cashed-up billionaires for the calcium components of my remains. Do I hear a starting bid of $1m?”

Jennifer Killen of St Peters has another regional first-time film (C8) experience: “My first visit to Leeton’s beautiful Roxy Theatre was a big adventure for a preschooler. I remember nothing of the movie which engrossed my mother and great-aunt, but the decades have not erased the memory of climbing up and over the seats behind, all the way until I reached the top. I then realised I could open the blinds and look out across the main street from above. Much more fun than watching the movie.”

“In the early ’50s, my parents, my brother and I went to the pictures every Saturday night in Marrickville,” recalls Dennis Fardy of Warriewood. “We had reserved seats and wore pyjamas and dressing gowns so we could go straight to bed on getting home. Ironically, the only movie I can remember from that time is The Robe.”

World.title: Toxic gas from rotting fish waste nearly killed two workers aboard fishing boat
World.content:
Two people almost died and three others were injured after being exposed to toxic gas from decomposing fish waste on a fishing boat docked in Canterbury.

Four workers were taken to hospital after rotten fish and water was accidentally pumped into a machinery space on the vessel in the dry dock at Lyttelton Port in February last year.

Two contractors performing routine maintenance on Antarctic Discovery were able to escape through the rotting fish waste but two crew who went to investigate were knocked unconscious by hydrogen sulphide released from the decaying fish.

The Transport Accident Investigation Commission has released its findings into the accident.

Acting chief investigator of accidents Tahlia Fisher said while the unintentional starting of an offal pump led to the accident, the investigation found four broader safety issues that also affected other industries.

"In this case, the bow thruster machinery space had the hazards and characteristics of an enclosed or confined space but hadn't been recognised and managed as one," she said.

"Where multiple organisations are operating in the same workplace there will be overlapping responsibilities and safety depends on active coordination between everyone working on site."

A near-fatal gas poisoning

Two apprentice fitters were working on a pipe tucked behind a tank that held a mixture of decaying fish waste and seawater.

The offal pump control panel had been painted over so the labels and indicator light that showed when it was running were not visible.

Investigators found it was "as likely as not" one of the fitters accidentally pressed the offal pump's start button causing the contaminated water from the holding tank to rain down on them.

The incident happened at Lyttelton Port in February last year. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

The two workers had no option but to climb up a ladder through the falling fish waste to escape to open air.

They were able to raise the alarm and the vessel superintendent entered the bow thruster room to investigate and was briefly overcome by hydrogen sulphide gas, a known by-product of decaying fish.

The chief engineer and second engineer came from another direction and collapsed. Crew used breathing apparatus to rescue the chief engineer, while the second engineer regained sufficient consciousness to crawl to safety.

Hydrogen sulphide is a colourless, flammable and highly-toxic gas known for its characteristic rotten egg smell at lower concentrations.

At high levels, people experience loss of smell, hindering detection, and exposure can be fatal in minutes due to respiratory failure.

The commission said multiple maritime safety agencies had issued warnings about decaying fish and seawater in refrigerated seawater tanks or fish holds could rapidly generate dangerous levels of hydrogen sulphide, especially at warmer temperatures, with fatalities often occurring during rescue attempts.

Failures that led to the fish waste overflow

A month before the accident, Antarctic Discovery was at sea when a valve for discharging fish waste from the tank at the front of the ship became blocked.

A temporary hose was used to pump waste to another tank. But it was mistakenly left connected to the offal pump with the open end tied to the ladder down into the bow thruster room.

The tank's outlet was left open and the offal pump was not isolated.

"In this case, the problem was not so much that one of the workers accidentally turned on the pump, it's the fact that the offal pumping system hadn't been deactivated correctly when it should have been," Fisher said.

The commission highlighted four safety issues:

the identification of hazards associated with confined or enclosed workspaces;

ensuring that machinery was safe prior to starting work;

following the correct processes when safety-critical systems are modified;

and when there were multiple parties on a shared worksite, ensuring each party was managing their risks appropriately.

Maritime NZ also investigated the accident and issued a warning, but wouldn't say to which company.

A spokesperson said it was a serious incident in which several workers were overcome by hydrogen sulphide, and it was relieved that all those affected had recovered.

"As the maritime regulator, we recommend ship operators, owners and maintenance workers understand the risks when working in confined spaces and have standard operating procedures to manage them.

"The incident had a range of parties involved from the owner of the vessel, the port, and contractors. All parties need to be aligned when it comes to understanding the risks and processes. If there are risks, such as with noxious gases, working in confined spaces can heighten these."

Changes made since the accident

The commission made recommendations to Australian Longline and Lyttelton Port Company to strengthen the management of its safety-critical systems and dry dock operations.

Australian Longline had since installed hydrogen sulphide detectors and cameras in the bow thruster room of Antarctic Discovery, along with sight glasses on the offal pump so the flow of waste could be observed when in use.

It had also bought hydrogen sulphide detectors for crew to wear and added the bow thruster room to the vessel's register of enclosed/hazardous spaces.

Australian Longline managing director Malcolm McNeill said the commission's inquiry was thorough and he appreciated the constructive nature of its findings and recommendations.

"Australian Longline remains committed to the ongoing review and continuous improvements of its safety management systems and operational procedures to ensure the safety of crew, contractors and all those who work alongside us," he said.

The commission found Lyttelton Port's safety standards and management of dry dock workers did not provide adequate protection from the accidental discharge of hazardous liquids and resulting gases.

No action had been taken to address the issue and it recommended the port company took steps to verify on-board systems with the potential to compromise safety were isolated and made safe prior to entering the dry dock and that awareness of the status of those systems was maintained during the vessel's time in the dry dock, the commission said.

It also recommended the company modify its processes to address how the overlapping responsibilities of parties conducting business in its dry dock were managed.

Lyttelton Port told the commission it was considering the recommendations.

Chief executive Graeme Sumner said it acknowledged the findings and recommendations in the report.

World.title: 40% of Kiwis taking on debt to cover increased living costs - Kiwibank
World.content:
The cost of living - and rising grocery bills in particular - is proving a big barrier to New Zealanders saving, according to a new report from Kiwibank.

The Kiwibank State of Savings Index, now in its third year, does a deep dive into New Zealanders' saving habits.

The nationwide survey was carried out by Talbot Mills Research.

It shows that while saving remains challenging, New Zealanders' budgeting and saving habits are holding steady.

This year's report found 44 percent of Kiwis regularly saved, compared with 43 percent last year.

Kiwibank chief executive Steve Jurkovich said the research showed that despite ongoing financial pressure, Kiwis continued to budget, save and find ways to make progress, from cutting spending to using new savings tools.

However, of those not saving, 61 percent said they could not save because they were prioritising surviving and could not make ends meet, while of those who reported saving challenges, 74 percent cited the cost of living as their biggest savings barrier.

Forty percent said they had taken on debt to cover increased living costs, with 19 percent turning to Buy Now, Pay Later schemes and 12 percent getting loans from family and friends.

"We are seeing a definite trend of people finding that they are having to turn to and use Buy Now, Pay Later in situations like supermarkets and other places where we probably didn't historically think that Buy Now, Pay Later would be showing up," Jurkovich said.

When it comes to financial emergencies, 28 percent of Kiwis said they would not have enough in their accounts to cover an unexpected bill of $500 without borrowing it, selling something, or putting it on a credit card.

The report found some groups faced greater pressures around savings than others.

For example, younger New Zealanders and renters were far more likely to have taken on debt to cover the cost of living, while Māori and Pacific peoples were significantly more likely to have taken on debt than NZ Europeans.

Kiwibank chief executive Steve Jurkovich. Supplied

Budgeting

The State of Savings report found 59 percent of Kiwis reported having a household budget, with 85 percent saying they broadly stick to it, up 1 percent from last year.

Thirty-nine percent made deliberate changes to improve savings, such as reducing discretionary spending, changing grocery shopping habits and cancelling subscriptions.

Steve Jurkovich said it showed the importance of building saving habits if people were able.

"It does really show, if you can just get started on that habit, that the habit sticks, and I 100 percent understand there are a bunch of people who wish they were in that position."

It also found that Kiwis were starting to turn to new tools to help with their budgeting and saving.

Twelve percent of those surveyed said they used AI for budgeting and savings advice, with 64 percent saying they thought it was helpful.

When it comes to savings products, only 54 percent said they were aware that savings accounts often require specific conditions to be met for customers to earn the headline interest rate.

The emergence of open banking was also starting to play a role in saving habits.

Open banking allows people to share their bank data with standalone financial apps and technology that can then make payments on their behalf.

World.title: Two years until 'one of most majestic sights' in Dunedin
World.content:
The countdown is on as Dunedin prepares for daytime darkness for the first time since 1163 AD.

On Wednesday at 4.15pm, the city marked exactly two years until the region's total solar eclipse when the moon's shadow passes directly over parts of Otago.

Claudia thought she would only see one eclipse in her lifetime.

She experienced one while working in a university hospital in Munich.

"Everybody stopped for the eclipse so the whole hospital stopped basically. No surgeries, no nothing, and we all walked out with our glasses to watch it," she said.

"Then it was dark, which was kind of beautiful but scary but weird. And then slowly the sun came back and we went back to work. But it was amazing. The whole hospital stopped."

She was walking her dog in Rotary Park as the city marked exactly two years until the eclipse.

That was where she planned to be on the day.

Tūhura Otago Museum director Dr Ian Griffin said eclipse chasers were already marking their calendars and booking trips.

"It's sudden and street lights come on and birds come home to roost and it becomes eerie and amazing," he said.

"What you see in the sky, it's like a hole in the sky. You see the black part, which is the moon covering the sun's disc, and around the sun is the solar corona which is this extended atmosphere and it's a beautiful thing to see, and it's one of the most majestic sights in nature."

The last solar eclipse visible in New Zealand was in 1965.

The eclipse would last about two hours, but there would only be about three minutes when the moon completely covered the sun.

He planned to watch it from his home on the Peninsula, which he bought 13 years ago partly with the eclipse in mind.

It would be far from his first eclipse, but certainly involved the least amount of travel.

In 2019, he flew to Tahiti and travelled on a boat for five days to experience an eclipse near the Pitcairn Islands.

"It was pouring with rain so having spent all that time and effort and money to get there, I was a bit disappointed," he said.

"But that being said, the sudden onset of darkness, even with rain and clouds and no sun visible, it was just extraordinary.

"I put it down as one of the most amazing times of my life."

Tūhura Otago Museim director Dr Ian Griffin described a total eclipse as one of the most majestic sights in nature. RNZ / Tess Brunton

Dunedin deputy mayor Cherry Lucas said it was a rare opportunity for the city.

"There are a lot of people who follow things like total eclipses and they're already booking accommodation. A lot of our accommodation providers are saying they've already got bookings more than two years out, which is exciting," she said.

"Some of our hospitality providers are already looking at offerings that will kind of feature the eclipse."

Dunedin deputy mayor Cherry Lucas said cities have come to a standstill during a total solar eclipse. RNZ / Tess Brunton

The city was already preparing for the eclipse with plans for a week long celebration from Matariki, she said.

"There could be like 30,000 people and I think because the eclipse is in a relatively narrow band through Otago and ... it's the school holidays, it gives people the opportunity to ... [either] fly or drive to Dunedin to be here to experience that," Lucas said.

"Cities literally come to a standstill while the eclipse happens and that is quite likely to happen here."

Dunedin House Boutique Hotel owner Anabel Tweedale was excited for what the eclipse would mean for the city.

"You're getting tourists that would never normally come to Dunedin, that would never of heard of Dunedin so I think that that's where it's so exciting to have such a great event that really showcases it," she said.

Dunedin House Boutique House owner Anabel Tweedale was keen for the city to celebrate the eclipse. RNZ / Tess Brunton

The hotel had not opened for 2028 bookings quite yet, but that was expected to happen over the next few months.

"We get so many tourists and travellers, they're only here for a night. They need to come for two, three, four nights because there's so much more to do and so many of our guests say 'we wish we'd stayed another night'," she said.

"That's what I think is so good about something like this. A week long festival or celebration would be just wonderful."

Dr Ian Griffin said there would need to be plenty of planning to make sure it all went ahead smoothly.

It was not like a concert - even though people were still talking about the traffic jams when thousands travelled to watch Pink perform in Dunedin, he said.

The eclipse was happening on a Saturday in the middle of the school holidays.

"In America in 2017 there was a solar eclipse that caused the biggest one day motion of traffic in a couple of state's history and they had all sorts of problems," he said.

"They ran out of petrol in the gas stations and the electric cars, there were only so many places for them to recharge."

World.title: LynnMall terrorist Ahamed Samsudeen threatened prison guards before attack, coroner told
World.content:
Ahamed Samsudeen called himself a terrorist and threatened guards while he spent time inside New Zealand's maximum security prison, a coroner has heard.

The inquest at the Auckland District Court has been told there was no programme to deradicalise Samsudeen while they had him in prison.

Shortly after his 2021 release, Samsudeen stabbed six shoppers at a West Auckland supermarket, before being shot dead by police.

Samsudeen was first arrested in 2017, charged with sharing violent ISIS videos, as well as possessing an offensive weapon, failing to assist police with a search, and using documents for financial gain.

He was bailed a year later, before being arrested again on a similar set of charges. It was during this time in prison where he was moved to the extreme risk unit inside Auckland's maximum security prison at Paremoremo.

Jeanette Burns, the commissioner for the extreme risk prisoners directorate, told the coroner about the behaviour that saw Samsudeen held in the unit.

"He was showing a pattern of escalating violence, escalating threats to staff, was claiming himself to be a terrorist and that he would come after staff if they didn't do what he wanted them to do," she said.

She was asked by stand-by counsel representing the interests of Samsudeen's family, Fletcher Pilditch KC, about the programmes for de-radicalisation available while Samsudeen was in custody.

"Was consideration given at the time of his management plan towards trying to find either a programme or some sort of tailored intervention to address the causes of why he was in remand in the first place?" Pilditch asked.

"In other words, his extremist beliefs, his ideologies, his threats of carrying out or acting out on the basis of his ideological beliefs."

Burns said there was no programme or treatment available at the time.

"Subsequently, our psychological services have been looking at different programmes," she said.

Dr Clarke Jones was the terrorism expert who designed a disengagement programme for Samsudeen in 2018.

His assessment of the future LynnMall attacker was scrutinised by Corrections counsel Lilla Dittrich, who asked if it had been limited by the secondary sources he was using.

"I think I would stand by my decisions of other action, or preventative action, could've been taken to address whatever level of mental health, problems with his mental should have been addressed earlier," he said.

Dr Jones said he stood by his opinion that Samsudeen's treatment while in custody contributed to his radicalisation, as opposed to rehabilitating him.

That was despite confirming he had never met the prisoner and was not involved with Samsudeen after 2018.

"Under the circumstances, I think I can make that statement because I know what the end result was," Jones said.

"Whether the treatment was effective and whether he was offered some sort of pre-release/post-release reintegration programme, then I would argue that the time in custody contributed to the outcome."

World.title: Whakatāne's loss, Masterton's gain: The musical chairs of medical scanning
World.content:
Whakatāne has waited years for a medical MRI scanner, but it has somehow ended up in Masterton.

Residents from the eastern end of Bay of Plenty must still travel to Tauranga for a scan in one of its seven MRI machines, all privately owned.

Health NZ says it is working on a plan for Whakatāne - but its last one failed.

June Goodhew says it has dragged on long enough.

In May, the 85-year-old retired tutor was given a packed lunch at Whakatāne Hospital and sat in an ambulance headed for Tauranga and an MRI.

She'd had septicemea.

A second woman sat up front.

"I really felt sorry for her because, you know, she was in pain," said Goodhew.

"From 11 o'clock till 5pm, it was quite a long day for people that are unwell. I imagine the cost of our travel, plus nurse and driver, would have been large, plus, well, not good for those in pain."

If Whakatāne had an MRI they could have just gone down the hall.

"This is the futility of all this nonsense of us getting it, promising and then we don't get it."

Whakatāne Hospital. Screenshot / Google

'Something went pear-shaped'

In 2014 Whakatāne Hospital got a $67 million upgrade, the government trumpeting about its "modern radiology department".

"This new building will ensure the 50,000 people living in the region continue to receive high quality health care for many years to come," said then health minister Tony Ryall.

Modern - but with no magnetic resonance imaging machine for advanced body scanning.

So locals tired of the 180km-round trip to Tauranga began pushing for one.

Several years later, Health New Zealand began talks with Bay Radiology, part of a big nationwide private provider RCHNZ Medical Imaging Group, majority owned by Infratil, to put its MRI in a yet-to-be built, specially designed unit at Whakatāne Hospital.

Dr Victor Luca, mayor at the time, anticipated it would be installed by the end of 2024.

"The territory had been defined, the building had been designed, site works were about to start."

But nothing happened.

"The end of 2024 came and went, 2025 came and went.

"We were all trying to uncover what had actually gone on ... obviously something went pear-shaped," said Luca.

Grey Power health campaigner Dr Victor Luca Supplied

'Relocated to Masterton'

Three months ago Health NZ Te Whatu Ora spelled it out to Whakatāne Action Group, which had emailed asking why the machine sat in a crate at Port Tauranga for a year.

"An agreement for a lease wasn't reached and the MRI has been relocated to Masterton. The MRI was owned by the private provider," the agency said.

HNZ told RNZ it terminated the deal with Bay Radiology over site constraints due to an earthquake faultline under parts of the hospital.

Authorities have known the fault was near the hospital since at least 2016.

More recently, they pinned down exactly where, and that area - where the MRI unit was to be - has now become an exclusion zone for new construction.

Health NZ said the existing hospital buildings were fine.

The Whakatāne Action Group said the agency had been helpful lately, but questioned why it did not find a suitable site in the first place.

Bay Radiology declined to comment about Masterton getting the machine or what it said were "'recollections, or assumptions".

"We appreciate the community's interest in this issue and understand the frustration many people feel," the company said in a statement.

"For some time, Bay Radiology has been seeking to work with Health New Zealand on an MRI service for Whakatāne.

"While we haven't reached an agreement on getting the MRI established yet, we hope we can progress this partnership opportunity to expand diagnostic imaging for the people of the Eastern Bays."

Wairarapa Hospital in Masterton. Supplied / Google Maps

New business case - but staffing hurdles

Asked if the Masterton machine was available for scans it funded in Wairarapa, HNZ said it did not know.

"The machine is privately-owned, as such we aren't privy to its current location or if it's being used in public or private care."

Luca has written twice in the local Beacon about what he calls "an absurd situation".

"My question is how the **** you get to the point of putting spades in the ground to be derailed by an earthquake fault that was known about in 2015?"

Health New Zealand said a new business case for MRI options for the eastern Bay community would be completed within the next three months.

It declined to be interviewed.

'Wage and workforce competition'

Staffing may still get in the way of the plans.

While HNZ had a new strategy to create a single, nationwide public radiology service, it had fewer than 350 radiologists to work with and increasingly they were spending more time in private clinics, according to workforce surveys. Technicians - MITs - were also in hot demand.

"We now have significant wage and workforce competition from private radiology for MITs that specialise in CT and MRI," said Health NZ on its website.

"This has led to some centres not operating public MRI machines due to workforce shortages."

The government this month passed a law making it explicit for Health New Zealand to work with private healthcare providers.

On the public front, Hawke's Bay hospital got a $35m-plus radiology upgrade last year.

On the private, RHCNZ has been targeting growth in "under-served regions, with plans to expand imaging services into Wānaka, Masterton, Palmerston North and Rangiora", according to Infratil's annual report. It did 10,000 more scans in 2025-26 than the previous financial year.

'We ... apologise for the inconvenience'

Last year Whakatāne protested over a downgrade of the hospital's obstetrics and gynaecology department due to lack of staff that forced hundreds of women from the Eastern Bay to travel to Tauranga Hospital to give birth. It staged a hikoi and secondary services were resumed in April 2026. However, a general manager appointed just last year had now resigned.

Five years back Tauranga had four MRI machines, now it had seven, all private.

Luca takes a bigger warning from the experience, a warning he and others of the town's Grey Power advocates made to health minister Simeon Brown in a face-to-face last year.

"All I can say is the present debacle indicates how difficult it is to do public-private partnership and it should be no mystery to anybody in New Zealand," said Luca.

He used the Official Information Act to find out $300,000 was spent a year on ambulances for Whakatāne MRI patients to go to Tauranga, at just under $500 dollars per trip.

People who were not admitted as patients had to find their own way.

The scans themselves cost the taxpayer $1100 each which was relatively cheap for an MRI.

"We acknowledge Dr Victor Luca's article and his concerns and apologise for the inconvenience caused to patients needing to travel," HNZ's group director of BOP operations Sarah Fenwick said in a statement.

It currently prioritised patients clinically to ensure those in greatest need were seen as quickly as possible, she said.

"We always work with patients to ensure they can access the services they need."

The action group said it continued to be involved in the push for an MRI.

June Goodhew would believe it when she saw it - she's even doubtful the faultline was really the problem HNZ made it out to be.

"That was the final excuse, I think, but then they didn't want to give up any of the parking area for the building.

"It's such a disappointment, and I think some of us suffer from a bit of anger, because why didn't we get it?

World.title: New Zealand 'on track for net zero', says prime minister
World.content:
The prime minister insists New Zealand will meet its climate change targets, despite a report saying they are very much at risk of being missed.

The Climate Change Commission's third annual monitoring report tracked New Zealand's progress in reducing emissions, as well as how it was tracking to meet its emissions goals.

The report showed time was running out to correct course, with the next 12 to 24 months critical to get things back on track.

But on Tuesday, prime minister Christopher Luxon said things were on track.

"Our view is based on the fact we're on track to deliver emissions budgets one and two. There's more work to do for emissions budget three and beyond, and our indications are we're on track for net zero. We may even do it a few years earlier."

The emissions budgets are the maximum quantity of emissions permitted over a five-year period. It has a sinking lid approach, with each budget setting a lower maximum.

Despite the prime minister's confidence, the commission said the current budget was at significant risk, and the subsequent one could not be met with current plans and policies.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said things had been on track, but the government had unwound that.

"We were making good progress until about 2024 as a country. The current government have wound back all of the things that were contributing to that progress. We've got to tackle our emissions, and it's actually good for New Zealanders. It's not only environmental benefits to it. There's cost of living benefits to it as well."

The commission's report noted the 2024 stalling was largely due to a dry year that meant coal was used to generate electricity.

The government has sought to address dry year risk, with its plans for a liquefied natural gas import terminal. Even then, the commission believed that would increase emissions, as it signalled delay to the transition from fossil fuels.

The commission said the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) was "not efficiently driving emissions reductions now, due to low market confidence, price volatility, and uncertainty about the long-term future of the scheme."

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick accused the government of being responsible for the falling confidence in the ETS.

"The government's absolutely screwed it," she said.

"The government has actively undermined confidence in the Emissions Trading Scheme, which also happens to be the only major tool that they have left for reducing emissions."

There are some things the government is doing that the commission has identified could reduce emissions, such as the Gas Transition Loan Scheme and time-of-use charges.

But the scales are tipped in the other direction, with policies like removing agriculture from the ETS, and committing to the LNG terminal.

The commission believed the ETS would need to be amended by 2030 in order for it to be effective.

But Hipkins did not seem keen on putting agriculture back into the scheme, instead preferring more investment in agri-tech.

"You're not going to bring down methane emissions just by saying, 'we must bring down methane emissions.' You actually have to support the technology, the science that allows you to do that."

The commission did identify some initiatives to get things back on track, like increased uptake of EVs and solar.

National, Labour, and the Greens are all proposing household solar at the election, highlighting the intersection between energy and cost of living policy.

Te Pāti Māori does not have a specific energy policy yet, but supports more regenerative and sustainable approaches.

Co-leader Rawiri Waititi said renewables would lift more people out of poverty.

"We've got a huge cost of living crisis at the moment when it comes to power, when it comes to fuel, when it comes to all of those types of things. And there's no strong move towards electrification of this country. Aotearoa should be the first electric country in the world."

New Zealand First wants to break up the gentailers, and identify and create a single dataset across oil, gas, geothermal, and carbon dioxide storages sites.

Deputy leader Shane Jones said there was "a lot of speculation" around climate change reporting thresholds, and expected climate change response and reforms would play a key part of the election campaign.

"No target should stand if it results in the impoverishment of New Zealand. No target should stand if it represents the hollowing out or the degradation of our industrial resilience. We've got to think about jobs and economic viability."

Earlier this week, the government announced a bail-out of up to $60 million to keep Golden Bay Cement's plant at Whangarei going.

Its owner, Fletcher Building, noted a "carbon cost disadvantage" Golden Bay Cement faced compared to imported cement.

ACT leader David Seymour said that was the bigger issue.

"We are now coming up against the reality, a lot of our competitors and friends around the world are not putting these costs onto business. Are we seriously saying we want New Zealand business to go out of business so that New Zealand consumers can pay to keep other people in jobs overseas?

"That's the reality that's hitting the road. I don't care what the Climate Change Commission is saying. They've been out of it for a long time."

Swarbrick suggested a fix through a climate border adjustment mechanism, such as the one the European Union applies.

She said the Greens had proposed such a mechanism in 2024, and also pointed to the party's energy policy released on Monday.

World.title: Cause of major IT outage across Waikato's hospitals remains unclear
World.content:
Staff at Waikato Hospital are recovering from the disruption caused by a major IT outage for hours on Wednesday.

Health NZ said late on Wednesday evening that the problem - which began at 10.44am - had been fixed, but it was contining to monitor the situation.

Thames, Te Kūiti, Tokoroa and Taumarunui hospitals were also affected.

The health agency has not said what exactly caused the problem, which meant longer wait times in the emergency department, some delayed surgeries, and forced staff to revert to paper systems.

Staff told RNZ patient history was limited to paper reports and any recent AI transcribed reports could not be accessed.

It also took longer to get test results and paging systems did not work.

Health NZ said it delivered safe patient care throughout the day.

"Any impact to clinical systems is treated with the greatest urgency. We reverted to manual processes for a number of areas such as patient information tracking and results reporting. Urgent care, including our Emergency Department, was prioritised with additional resource in place."

World.title: AI is changing the way consumers shop, and businesses need to get ready
World.content:
For years, consumers have discovered products and made purchase decisions by using search engines, websites, or recommendations from family and friends.

Enter artificial intelligence. The technology that has already changed so much, is also transforming shopping.

Research by PwC has found that AI tools have become the third most-used channel for product research among consumers, behind search engines and retailer websites or apps.

PwC's survey of 1000 consumers found 44 percent said AI had reduced their use of search engines when researching purchases.

PwC partner Phil Wheeler said it was an important finding, and highlighted the start of an evolution for consumers.

"They are using it primarily at the moment for the early stages of that shopping journey," he said.

It meant consumers were using AI for product inspiration, comparison, price options and price benefits, rather than executing the purchase itself.

PwC partner Phil Wheeler. Supplied / PwC

"We think that [the latter point] is really related to trust in AI, and the evolution of AI -- I mean it's not perfect yet, there's still development going on," he said.

Wheeler said businesses had to act to get on top of changing consumer behaviour.

"I think for consumer brands and retailers, they now need to start committing to adapting the way that they present in the market," he said.

"That's no longer adapting it for [just] search engine optimisation ... or social media."

Wheeler said it had become "how does AI view me as a brand or what type of perception is it going to provide to consumers when they search or prompt a particular product?".

The PwC report said for businesses it raised questions around the discoverability of their products and services within AI-driven experiences, and whether their production information was structured, accurate and trusted.

And it raised a question of how marketing and online strategies should evolve if consumers bypassed traditional search methods.

PwC said the next phase of the AI evolution was already emerging, with AI agents able to act on a consumer's behalf, from comparing products to completing purchases.

Its report said while agentic commerce was in its early stages, its findings suggested adoption was already underway.

World.title: Eels defend Luai's 2027 signing ahead of Chiefs move
World.content:
Parramatta coach Jason Ryles says he is unapologetic about agreeing to Jarome Luai's one-season stopover at the Eels.

Luai, who is the PNG Chiefs' marquee recruit for 2028, last week signed with the Eels for next season.

A four-time premiership winner with the Panthers, Luai was released by Wests Tigers, which want to give their younger halves opportunities in first grade.

Ryles said he had no concerns Luai's arrival would discourage Parramatta's halves prospects.

Luai joins Parramatta, Marshall slams relationship breakdown rumours Benji Marshall has slammed "bull**** rumours" claiming a fractured relationship with Jarome Luai contributed to the star five-eighth's early exit from Wests Tigers.

He said signing Luai was a win for the 15th-placed Eels' stable of younger halves options, which includes Joash Papalii, Lincoln Fletcher and Lorenzo Talataina.

"We're sitting in a spot on the ladder that we don't want to be," Ryles said.

"It's no-one's fault directly but we need more experienced players. Jarome fits that bill at the moment.

"We have got younger players that are coming through our pathways and our system that may be ready in 12 months.

"But this gives them an extra bit of time to … learn off a true pro that's won a lot of premierships."

Amid a season of injury concerns for the Eels, centre Will Penisini could return from osteitis pubis via reserve grade this weekend.

Ryles said he was hopeful veteran prop Junior Paulo and outside back Bailey Simonsson would be back from their long-term injuries in "the next one or two weeks".

AAP

World.title: Lewis breaks Australian 100m record, beats five-time Olympic champ
World.content:
Torrie Lewis has set a new Australian women's 100 metres record after breaking her own national record at a meet in Slovakia.

Lewis ran a time of 11.04 seconds, beating her previous record time of 11.08 as she beat out Jamaica's five-time Olympic champion Elaine Thompson-Herah, who finished in second.

The 21-year-old Lewis also competed in and won the 200m event, where she ran a 22.66.

It is the third separate time Lewis has broken the Australian 100m record, having previously done so as a 19-year-old in 2024 by running an 11.10 before lowering that mark to 11.08 at last year's World Championships.

Lewis beat out Jamaican sprint icon Elaine-Thompson Herah (pictured). (Getty: Al Bello)

Lewis made her Olympic debut in the 200m event in Paris two years ago and finished in the semifinals after running a then-personal-best time of 22.89. She also competed in the 4x100m event in Paris.

The women's 100m record is owned by late American sprint legend Florence Griffith-Joyner, who ran a 10.49 at the US Olympic trials in 1988. Thompson-Herah holds the second-fastest 100m mark of all time at 10.54.

Griffith-Joyner also holds the world record for the 200m, 21.34, a mark she set at the 1988 Olympics in Seoul.

Both records are among the longest-standing across all women's athletics.

The career-best 100m time comes at the perfect time for Lewis, who is poised to compete in the 100m, 200m and 4x100m relay events at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

World.title: Fox sisters combine in 'dream team' for gold medals at World Championships
World.content:
The gold rush at the world titles has continued for Jess Fox, with the canoe slalom legend spearheading the Australian women's kayak team to victory in Oklahoma.

A day after three-time Olympic champion Fox claimed gold in the kayak cross time trial event, the 32-year-old joined her younger sister Noemie Fox and Kate Eckhardt at the top of the podium.

The victory at Riversport Rapids on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST) continued Fox's successful return to competition since undergoing surgery to remove a tumour from a kidney last August.

Loading Instagram content

It is the second title for the trio after winning gold in London in 2023 in the same event, which is only contested at the world championships.

Competing on the same course that will host the canoe slalom at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, the Australians used experience and expertise in their clinical run to put pressure on the final three teams.

In third place heading into the final third of the race, the trio lifted to complete a clean run through the gates and finish 0.64 seconds ahead of France and Slovakia.

"We're a bit of a dream team," Noemie said.

"We've been training so well and supporting each other. There was so much trust and support in the lead in, and we felt so good and wanted to do our best out there.

"To share these moments and be so proud of what we've done and to have those moments in an individual sport where we can collectively push each other and celebrate together is so special.

"It was just so much fun out there and to be rewarded with a gold medal is amazing, and I'm so proud of our double title now."

The golden girls also had success in the individual kayak race, with all qualifying for the top 30 semifinals.

Despite posting the fastest time of the day, Jess Fox, who is chasing a 16th world title, was docked for two gate touches and progressed in ninth place.

Jess Fox is chasing a 16th world title. (ABC News: Sean Tarek Goodwin)

"A bit of a shaky start with the two touches back-to-back, but overall it was then solid and I kept the boat speed on and I knew I would have to push to qualify because you never know — that top 30 can be really tight especially on a course like this," she said.

Eckhardt qualified in 11th position and Noemie was 25th.

In the men's kayak teams final, the Australian men had an unfortunate 50-second penalty in their run and finished 18th.

They had better luck in the individual kayak heats, with all six paddlers progressing through to the K1 semi-finals.

Olympian Tim Anderson was the best of the Aussies in eighth.

AAP

World.title: Former Socceroos captain Paul Wade reveals probable CTE diagnosis
World.content:
Former Socceroos captain Paul Wade has revealed he has been diagnosed with "probable" chronic traumatic encephalopathy, which has been linked to repeated head knocks and injuries.

In a statement put out by Professional Footballers Australia (PFA) on Wednesday, Wade said he was diagnosed in late 2024 with a suspected case of the disease after experiencing neurological symptoms.

He said this was upgraded after further assessments to probable in 2025.

The disease can only be confirmed after death.

"They did the tests … and [the neurologists] went, 'Oh, we've got a real problem here'," he told the ABC.

Symptoms of the disease can include depression, memory loss, tremors, poor impulse control and suicidal thoughts.

After scans showed it was probable CTE he said he just "stood there" and thought "am I going to die from this?"

Wade revealed a diagnosis of probable chronic traumatic encephalopathy. (7.30)

Wade's neurologist Rowena Mobbs made the "probable" diagnosis after two years of monitoring his symptoms and extensive testing.

Dr Mobbs said neurologists across Australia started using "probable" diagnoses to refer patients to the right treatment.

"It's not about fear, it's not about giving any definitive diagnosis, but it's about getting appropriate care and support to people," she said.

"I think Paul and his family want to see people in the community feeling confident that they can come forward for help and getting that right dementia care."

'He knew something was wrong'

Wade, who now lives on the Central Coast, north of Sydney, said receiving the diagnosis was "difficult" but wanted to share his experience to raise awareness of concussion and brain health across all levels of football.

"Football gave me so much. It gave me a life, a career, incredible experiences and the privilege of representing Australia," he said.

" But I also must be honest about the challenges I now face and the uncertainty that comes with living with a neurodegenerative condition. "

Asked whether the probable diagnosis was linked to his time playing, he said "it must have had something to do with it".

"I think about the number of times at a training session I headed a ball."

Dr Mobbs said Wade expressed a level of "validation" when he received the "probable" diagnosis.

"He knew it in himself… He knew something was wrong, he knew it felt different," she said.

Head of neuropathology at Sydney's Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, Michael Buckland, said a "probable" CTE diagnosis should be used for research purposes rather than in a clinical context.

"We have no idea how accurate that [diagnosis] is, it's still being tested," he said.

"The authors of the paper, that defined what probable CTE is, strongly cautioned against using it in a clinical setting, and they and others recognise the real risk of harm in giving someone a diagnosis that you can't really be confident about."

However, Dr Buckland commended Wade for raising awareness of the condition.

"I think he's done a very generous and courageous thing by speaking publicly," Dr Buckland said.

Doctor urges ban to headers by children

Rowena Mobbs said Wade's diagnosis came after "extensive testing". (ABC News: Michael Nudl)

After 30 years of exposure to head knocks in soccer, including headers, Dr Mobbs said repetitive traumatic brain injury was the "main burden" for Wade.

Dr Mobbs urged Football Australia to ban headers for children playing soccer under the age of 12.

"We must hold onto our activity and sport in life, for our kids especially, but we need to lower the repetitive head injury burden," she said.

"That's where we need good care in the community, with our excellent health systems, the government to step in and provide funding for research, and for us all to be aware of our lifetime burden of head injury and try and prevent it where possible."

Sixty-four-year-old Wade, who led the national team for six years in the 1990s, said more understanding was needed about the long-term effects of repeated head impacts to "protect future generations".

"If sharing my experience can help someone seek support, create better education and prevention, or help the game take brain health more seriously, then it is worth doing," Wade, who also lives with epilepsy, said.

'Advancement of the game'

Wade's announcement comes less than a month after Four Corner's revealed 33 Australian Rules players had been diagnosed with CTE.

Wade (left) leading out the Socceroos for the 1993 Australia v Argentina FIFA World Cup play-off match. (Getty Images: Joe Mann/Offside)

He said people concerned should not stop playing contact sports "because if you do we're going to have an even bigger problem with mental health and wellbeing".

"To the people actually making the rules we've got to come up with ways we can make it safer," Wade said.

"If I could say to Football Australia, or even FIFA, if you're listening, let's put some protocols in there because you've got everything about concussion.

"[But] you don't talk about CTE and how we can change the game and change the training and change the age so that it's minimalised, so we're not exposing kids to CTE."

He asked who was going to "stand up and be brave and say no", and assert boundaries.

"Someone's got to say no. Kids are … heading a ball 12 years or under. Make it 14, I don't care," he said.

PFC Chair Francis Awaritefe urged sporting organisations to ban heading for young players, particularly until children learn the "proper technique".

"We shouldn't even be waiting, I think we should be doing it now," Mr Awaritefe said.

PFA chief executive Beau Busch said Wade's decision to open up about his diagnosis was an "important act of leadership".

"In sharing his story Paul has once again illustrated his truly remarkable commitment to the advancement of the game," Mr Busch said.

"He is doing so not only for himself but for the players and families who are facing, or may one day face, similar questions about brain health."

Mr Busch said Australian football must be proactive in tackling brain injuries "through better policies, research, education and support for former players".

A decorated career

Wade, who was born in England in 1962, came to Australia at 11 years of age with a passion for football, moving his way up to senior positions within Victorian clubs including Croydon, Green Gully, Brunswick and South Melbourne.

In 1985 he claimed a spot in the Australian team, playing his first full international against Czechoslovakia the following year.

He then captained the Australian soccer side from 1990 to 1996.

Wade was captain of the Socceroos for six years. (News Video)

On Football Australia's website Wade is credited with 345 national league appearances, 119 matches played for Australia, and 84 full internationals.

Wade also played in the 1988 Olympic Games and two World Cup qualifying campaigns.

After he retired as a player he became involved with TV commentary and coaching clinics for kids.

His career and the impacts of his neurodegenerative condition will be explored in an upcoming mini documentary being produced by PFA.

World.title: Spanish chief accuses FIFA boss of 'destroying the football industry'
World.content:
Gianni Infantino should resign as head of FIFA for "destroying the football industry" by expanding international competitions, according to Javier Tebas, the president of Spain's football league La Liga

It is not the first time he has lashed out at Infantino over fixture congestion and for considering a proposal to expand the 2030 men's World Cup from 48 teams to 64.

"Increasing the number of national teams makes no sense. The football industry isn't just the World Cup, which is the most important event. But not everything can revolve around the World Cup," Tebas told La Gazzetta dello Sport.

Players and fans made the World Cup a success, but the politics shouldn't be forgotten The biggest ever World Cup brought diverse communities together and galvanised its non-traditional footballing co-hosts, but the concerns raised from the start have not disappeared in the positive afterglow.

"In my opinion, yes, I think his time is up," he said of Infantino. "However, he has the support of the system and the federations, so there's not much more to add, is there? There's no opposition candidate, nobody wants to stand just to lose. This is the system and it's rotten at its core.

"He shouldn't stay, but he won't leave. I've heard many people who are against Infantino. They say it, but then they do nothing. I don't know what's worse, the silence or the complicity, because those who stay silent are perfectly aware of the damage football is suffering."

South American soccer's ruling body CONMEBOL has made an official proposal to expand the 2030 World Cup to 64 teams. The competition is already set to be the most sprawling edition, with six host nations spread across three continents.

"It's national competition that sustains this sport," Tebas added. "They are destroying the football industry, which generates tens of thousands of jobs, for an event that lasts 40 days and involves a minority of players."

The World Cup final had a 27-minute half-time interval thanks to a half-time show featuring artists such as Justin Bieber (pictured). (Reuters: Amanda Perobelli)

He also criticised world football's governing body FIFA over the new hydration breaks implemented at the World Cup, which ended on Sunday, as well as the extended 27-minute half-time interval — rather than the standard 15 — during the final, in which Spain defeated Argentina 1-0.

The hydration breaks midway through each half were introduced to help players deal with the summer heat in the United States, Canada and Mexico. But critics say they had unintended consequences, ruining the flow of the game and giving coaches a chance to tactically shift momentum in their team's favour.

"FIFA arranges things as it pleases, for what it wants, for its own interests, certainly not for football," Tebas said. "Hydration breaks are a lie. We have them in La Liga, but only when it's genuinely hot. Here, the pitches in Dallas, Los Angeles, and Atlanta had air conditioning. It was a lie and just a break for advertising."

Infantino announced in April that he would run for re-election for a fourth term as president. The vote for the 2027–2031 period is scheduled for March 18 in Morocco.

La Liga boss Javier Tebas has not been shy about attacking Infantino in the past. (Getty Images: Oscar J. Barroso/Europa Press)

The Football Supporters Europe (FSE) group also called on the wider soccer community to hold FIFA to account.

In a statement on its website headlined "A World Cup that failed supporters", the FSE demanded "structural governance reforms to hand decision-making power back to the FIFA Council and Congress and ensure full consultation with clubs, leagues, players and supporters".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

It added: "The 2026 World Cup should have been a celebration of the game and the supporters who give it life. Instead, it has too often become a case study in what is so deeply wrong with football today.

"From the outset, supporters were asked to place their trust in FIFA and "chill", but it prioritised spectacle and commercialisation over the match-going experience with key elements of football's identity being messed with. Over the last month, we've seen football contorted to the whim of Gianni Infantino and the Trump administration."

The FSE, accepted by European soccer's governing body UEFA as the recognised group representing fans in the region, then went on to attack "historically high ticket prices" and "skyrocketing transportation costs, bending of rules and procedures, exclusion of swathes of the global population and a lack of transparent communication".

"All this created an environment of confusion and distrust that has severely damaged the reputation of FIFA, the World Cup, and the integrity of football itself," its statement said.

"The lessons from this World Cup are clear: FIFA is unfit to govern global football. The future of the game cannot rest in the hands of a man who has proven yet again that he puts financial and political interests ahead of the future of our game."

AP

World.title: Cameron McEvoy has lived a life between trips to Glasgow
World.content:
When Cameron McEvoy travelled to Glasgow in 2014, he was a 19-year-old "kid".

Twelve years later, he returns to the site of his Commonwealth Games debut as a completely different man with a completely different outlook on a sport that is almost unrecognisable.

McEvoy emerged as part of the ill-fated batch of sprint stars at the 2012 Olympics — the so-called "weapons of mass destruction" who returned from London without a gold medal from any male swimmer.

Two years later, McEvoy won six medals, including two relay golds, at the Commonwealth Games despite still trying to find his place in the squad.

"I still felt like a new person on the team back in 2014," he told reporters at Glasgow airport on Wednesday morning (AEST).

Cam McEvoy says his 50m freestyle world record is just the beginning When Cameron McEvoy broke the long-standing 50m freestyle world record in March, he was at great pains to note that he believes he can go even faster.

"I was super shy; I wasn't really outspoken. I'm in the same sport but the way I'm conducting training on a day-to-day basis, the way being on the team feels now compared to as a rookie, almost feels like it's a new sport.

"It's going to be almost nostalgic being back at the Tollcross pool, seeing the set-up and going through the same thing I did as a teenager."

As he and the Dolphins touched down in the Scottish capital once again, McEvoy is a brand new man and one of only two Australian swimmers, along with Lakeisha Patterson, back for another go.

"A lot has changed," he said.

"I was basically a kid [in 2014], and now I've got my own kid. Things are very different now.

A baby-faced McEvoy won three individual silvers as part of a six-medal haul in Glasgow 12 years ago. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"There's actually a member on the swim team who's 14 [Mia Hogan], so she was only two when I was back here competing last time.

"A lot has happened; basically, my entire international career has unfolded."

Do you know an athlete competing at the Commonwealth Games? Share with us Whether you are you a family member, a friend, a colleague or a coach, share your connection with us and how you will be supporting them.

McEvoy missed out on individual medals at his first three Olympic Games and is surprisingly still hunting his first individual Commonwealth gold.

At Glasgow 2014 he finished second in the 50m, 100m and 200m. At his home Games on the Gold Coast in 2018, the pain was amplified when he picked up bronze in the 50m but missed the medals in the 100m despite entering as the Commonwealth record holder and fastest qualifier for the final.

McEvoy struggled to bounce back from those setbacks, particularly at Rio 2016 and Gold Coast 2018, to the point that when the last Commonwealth Games were on, he was at home considering his future in the sport.

He said he was "in the wilderness", unsure if he wanted to continue swimming after so many painful disappointments, but teammate Elijah Winnington's mental resilience got him back in the pool.

"Elijah had just won the 400m freestyle world title on the back of falling short in Tokyo [2021 Olympics]. For me, I saw that as a massive inspiration," he said.

"I fell short in Rio and couldn't bounce back that following year, but seeing Elijah go from Tokyo seventh in the 400m final to world champion, that was definitely a factor in motivating me to want to take that next step and come back."

ABC Sport will be live blogging every day of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

World.title: US rider hit by car in road rage incident before Tour de France time trial
World.content:
American rider Brandon McNulty was apparently involved in a road rage incident before the time trial stage of the Tour de France.

McNulty, a teammate of overall race leader Tadej Pogačar, was confronted by an angry motorist who overtook him on his way to the start of stage 16, Mauro Gianetti, the CEO of UAE Emirates XRG, told broadcaster Eurosport.

Gianetti said the driver of the car was furious and that he stopped his vehicle after overtaking McNulty, who then collided with the vehicle.

"He was just coming to the start with the bike. One car was a little bit upset behind him; we don't know why, and then he overtook Brandon, and he stopped the car. Unfortunately, of course, Brandon crashed into the car," he said.

"Apparently it's nothing so big and all good, but it was not nice. Yes, it was a car from the public, and we don't know."

Time-trial champ wins back-to-back stages

Time trial world champion Remco Evenepoel was fastest as he won the 16th stage of the Tour de France to shave 28 seconds off Tadej Pogačar's commanding lead.

Evenepoel completed the 26.1-kilometre individual time trial in 32 minutes, 19 seconds, more than a minute faster than Mattias Skjelmose, the previous quickest, before the Belgian rider waited to see Pogačar cross the line with the second-best effort of the day.

It is the third year straight that Evenepoel has won a time trial at the Tour. His parents and family members were present on Belgium's national holiday to see him take back-to-back stage victories after winning the 15th stage on Sunday. Monday was a rest day.

His teammate Florian Lipowitz crashed out, however. The German rider slipped going around a sharp bend toward the finish and slid across the road into the sidewalk kerb. He was unable to continue with what looked like a shoulder injury.

"It's a bittersweet pill to swallow with this victory. I wish him all the best, and I hope he's not too bad," Evenepoel said of his Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe teammate. "I will really miss him for the whole week."

Paxti Vila, director sportif of the Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team, had mixed feelings after the stage.

"On one side, you're happy because we won, but on the other side, you are kind of sad because Florian had that crash at kilometre 19.8 on that right turn," Vila said. "He's still on the way to the hospital. Let's see when the medical update arrives."

Pogačar survives scare

Pogačar had a wobble going around the same corner where Lipowitz crashed but recovered to continue.

The four-time Tour champion leads second-place Evenepoel by 4 minutes, 32 seconds with five stages remaining.

"Tadej is on his way to win a fifth Tour de France," Evenepoel said of a feat that would move the Slovenian rider level with Belgium's Eddy Merckx, Spain's Miguel Indurain and French riders Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault.

"I think it's just amazing that I can be a bit close to him," he said of Pogačar. "It's an honour to race with him … so, for me, it's a big step forward that I can at least be a bit around him, and I try to learn from him."

AP

World.title: Players and fans made the World Cup a success, but the politics shouldn't be forgotten
World.content:
The past six weeks across the USA, Canada and Mexico have been so full of life, colour, controversy, and chaos that the longest men's World Cup in history feels like it has zipped past all too fleetingly.

The 'sad Pablo Escobar' memes are now in overdrive in social media algorithms that have been contorted into a daily World Cup newsfeed delivered in a very 2026 way.

Loading Instagram content

It is very likely that even if you were not a fan beforehand, you at least know about the Viking row, the Tartan Army, that Cabo Verde is a country and one that is quite good at football, and basically everything and anything about Erling Haaland.

Whether consumed through meme form, subtle second screening while at work, watch parties, or attending live, this tournament has delivered on its promise of capturing the world's attention.

But mega sporting events always do that, so how was this one any different, and what sort of legacy will it come away with?

Bringing people together

FIFA President Gianni Infantino is a hype master and summed it up in spectacularly hyperbolic terms.

"This World Cup has not just broken all possible records, it has smashed them. It has destroyed every record," he said after Spain's victory in the final.

Spain celebrates winning its second men's World Cup trophy. (Getty Images: Alex Livesey-Danehouse)

"The official figures will come out soon, but probably over 6 billion people watching it from home. The world was standing still.

"I think we have to invent a new vocabulary, new words to define the success of this World Cup."

For now, we will go with the words we have.

Infantino is right about the omnipresence of this World Cup in powerful and unexpected ways.

It is no surprise that competing countries and diaspora communities were entranced by following their nation, with emotive scenes playing out all around the world as they lived and breathed their teams' campaigns, including in Australia.

Many Socceroos fans travelled to North America to follow the team. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

What was more evocative was the people who, on face value, had no real connection to the participating teams but felt drawn to them for their own varying reasons.

Like the pictures from Gaza of Palestinians supporting Egypt against Argentina in the round of 16, whilst sitting on the rubble of destroyed buildings.

Palestinians gathered among buildings destroyed by Israeli strikes to cheer on Egypt against Argentina. (Getty Images: Saeed M. M. T. Jaras)

Or the way the small Midwest town of Lawrence, Kansas, wholeheartedly embraced hosting the Algerian team who set up base camp there.

Dr Lindsay Sarah Krasnoff, from New York University's Tisch Institute for Global Sport, is an expert in sports diplomacy, and said connections between fans and communities would provide an important legacy.

"Small acts of sports diplomacy, particularly on a citizen-to-citizen level, add up and move mountains," she said.

Mexico fans were ubiquitous throughout North America. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

"However, I think it's important to note that it is not a magic wand. Sports diplomacy by itself cannot instantly fix things. It's not going to create world peace overnight. It's not going to resolve terse political, financial or other policy differences.

"But it does have that ability — once you interact with someone through sport — you understand a little bit more about them.

"And you'll also realise that there's a lot more that binds us together … than what sets us apart.

Dr Krasnoff added that players and national teams could help create change through their presence on the global stage.

Iraq played in its first World Cup since 1986. (Getty Images/FIFA: Maddie Meyer)

"Up until this summer's tournament, most of the Western and particularly the Anglophone press, whenever we've heard about Iraq over the last 20, 30 years, it's usually been in a very negative connotation," she said.

"Related to civil war, religious fundamentalism, bombing. However, by being part of the select 48 who were able to qualify for the tournament, they showed that they are just like everyone else in the world."

But as this tournament unfolded, two more people were shot and killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in separate incidents in Maine and Houston.

A phone call, making money, and going big

The biggest controversy of the tournament centred on the US President Donald Trump and a phone call to his friend.

The leader of one of the host countries freely admitted to calling FIFA president Infantino to ask for a favour for star American player Folarin Balogun to have his suspension wiped out.

US President Donald Trump presented Spain with the trophy after its victory. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

FIFA insisted it was an above-board process undertaken by its independent disciplinary committee, but this is an issue which will not wash away in the positive afterglow of this tournament, and is still being probed.

It would be fair to say the hosting across three countries and expanded 48-team format was broadly a success.

There were no excessive blowouts, some all-time classics, stirring underdog tales and new heroes emerged.

On the flip side, there were some rather forgettable clashes thrown in, and the days with six games felt like too much, even for the most passionate fans.

But with broadcast deals its biggest source of revenue, there is no way FIFA will turn back to 32 teams now, although it could expand even further in four years' time.

Argentina's Lionel Messi had a brilliant tournament. (Getty Images: Tom Weller)

"The next one is at home! In 2030, the World Cup is coming to Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay," CONMEBOL President Alejandro Dominguez wrote on social media.

"It will ‌be ⁠a great opportunity for football, to celebrate the World Cup's centenary with a 64-team tournament."

FIFA has not confirmed the format for 2030, although it runs the risk of having too much of a good thing should it go down that path.

The ticket prices were another hot topic; ultimately, the market justified the inflated prices, as most stadiums were filled across the 104 matches.

But it is also worth pointing out that many of the atmospheres inside were not always the frenzied fever pitch that might be experienced in top domestic leagues.

At times the venues were more akin to the Super Bowl, where the diehards could not make it in, only those with the deepest wallets.

Whether or not you think that matters, all comes down to perspective.

The excessive heat was dangerous for players and fans at times, not helped by most marquee games kicking off in the afternoon, to accommodate European TV viewing schedules.

And the mandatory hydration breaks, while needed on a 40-degree day in Miami or Philadelphia, were laughable in an air-conditioned Atlanta or Dallas Stadium.

The match between France and Paraguay in Philadelphia was played in stifling heat. (Getty Images: FIFA/Maddie Meyer)

"I think we've seen up close and from the front row, FIFA diplomacy at work, in a wide variety of different ways, the good, the bad and everything in between," Dr Krasnoff said.

"And there's also likely a lot going on beneath the surface that hasn't yet made its way into the public spotlight.

"I think this was perhaps a rapid-fire immersion in the world of FIFA and how FIFA is its own entity. And sometimes things are not necessarily always as logical as one would think."

The greatest successes and positives of this tournament came from the players and the football being played on the pitch, and the fans who embraced it so wholeheartedly.

Curaçao Livano Comenencia celebrated scoring his country's first ever World Cup goal. (Getty Images: Alexander Hassenstein)

From the smallest nation to ever qualify, Curaçao, scoring its first World Cup goal, to 40-year-old Cabo Verde goalkeeper Vozinha becoming an international treasure, to the phenomenal feats of current greats like Lionel Messi, Kylian Mbappé, Haaland, Harry Kane, and the Spanish team.

And the scenes of the Dutch Oranje walk taking over Texas, Mexicans in literally every single North American city outnumbering any other fan in huge numbers, or Egyptians celebrating a loss as if it was one of their greatest victories.

Thousands of Dutch fans took part in the Oranje Fanwalk ahead of all their games. (Reuters: Joseph Buvid)

But this does not automatically absolve the key powerbrokers or negate the legitimate concerns and issues that were raised in the lead-up and throughout.

It just means the football did the talking for the most part as it usually does, and now the rest will come back into play.

Soccer converts

The bigger question of the legacy in North America, particularly in Canada and the USA where 'soccer' is not number one, is more difficult to answer in the immediate aftermath.

The conversation is different in Mexico, where football's status as number one has never been questioned, although its legacy will be tangled up in the immense cost to co-host, and whether it was worth it as it continues to deal with serious social issues.

Canadians watched and attended in record numbers, as the team had its best result, making it to the round of 16.

This was Canada's most successful men's World Cup campaign. (Getty Images: Fran Santiago)

Their engagement with the tournament is not overly surprising in a country where ice hockey is linked to its identity, but football is the number one participation sport.

"When you start seeing these top-level performances, say making it to the top 16 or coming top four or [the women's team] winning gold at the Olympics, in a sport so competitive as soccer, it has a different reckoning, I think for the audience and certainly for Canada," Dr Nicole Forrester from Toronto Metropolitan University said.

"If we're talking about the emotional impact and the intangible piece to it, I think it would be interesting to track how our athletes, our male athletes in particular, fare in future major international competitions.

"And with our audience in terms of how much we get behind, not just supporting, but perhaps there might be a shift where there's [more] expectation."

Major League Soccer (MLS) is already in overdrive trying to capitalise on the commercial success of the tournament and convert it to eyeballs on the domestic product.

The organisation has said it wants to become one of the best leagues in the world, alongside Europe's top five.

That is a big, bold ambition, and would need a lot more Messi/Inter Miami partnerships to bring that to fruition.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

And while travelling fans and immigrant communities were always going to be swept up in the game here, the non-traditional football fans are the ones that now need to be converted.

Of the three co-hosts, the USA was always going to be the most scrutinised as a world superpower and hosting the most games.

Throughout the US, I spoke to countless locals who did not consider themselves football fans but were excited by the energy and buzz around their city hosting a World Cup.

They now need to hold onto that feeling and watch more games on TV and attend MLS and National Women's Soccer League matches.

Right now, there is still a high, a palpable buzz from having pulled off the most ambitious staging of the biggest standalone sporting event in the world.

But it is what comes next that will be most telling.

Tech.title: Apple is reportedly testing a MacBook Neo with more RAM
Tech.content:
Following the MacBook Neo’s huge popularity so far, Apple is reportedly developing an updated version of its budget laptop with a new processor and more memory, and even has plans to refresh the model with new colors. Following a similar report from analyst Tim Culpan earlier this year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says the new Neo will run on an A19 Pro processor, which currently powers the iPhone 17 Pro / Pro Max and the iPhone Air, unlike the current laptop’s A18 Pro that was originally in the iPhone 16 Pro. The chip upgrade also means the updated Neo may have more RAM, likely 12GB rather than the original 8GB.

However, ongoing component shortages will almost certainly mean the next Neo costs more than the original did, previewed by Apple raising prices on nearly all of its devices last month. Another way it could get more expensive to start is the possibility that Apple could discontinue the lowest-priced 256GB version of the Neo.

In addition to rumors of an updated Neo, Gurman also says Apple is planning to release new iMacs, which last got a refresh in 2024, with OLED screens. Other long-rumored updates like the M6 MacBook Pro and OLED touchscreen MacBooks are also reportedly on the way, with the OLED models coming sometime late this year or early next year, as well as a newly redesigned base model 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M7 chip inside for next year.

Tech.title: Here’s what Samsung’s smart glasses actually look like
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Samsung has given us our first chance to check out its upcoming smart glasses in person, revealing two new designs and the first specs in the process, including an impressive 9-hour battery life. The glasses, developed in collaboration with Google and the eyewear brands Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, are due to launch this fall.

Google and Samsung have been teasing the new glasses for some time, and revealed the first two designs at I/O in May. Now there are two more frames: Both are unsurprisingly boxy, with a new set of squared off black glasses from Gentle Monster, and a more rounded, red-brown pair from Warby Parker. Jaein Choi, the executive vice president running Samsung’s mobile experience division, told CNBC that there are “more designs” on the way.

This was our first chance to see any of the four frames in person, though Samsung wouldn’t let me try them on — or even hold them up to my face. They’re all impressively light — not much heavier than the thick-rimmed acrylic glasses I used to wear, and barely bigger than them either. Speaker and microphone grilles are hidden along the stems, a single button sits on the right with a power switch tucked inside on the left, and of course there’s a camera and recording LED mounted on the front. Much like Meta’s collaborations with Ray-Ban and Oakley, these basically look like normal glasses most people would happily wear — privacy connotations aside.
